title: A gentle introduction to lattice-based cryptography
abstract: We present four quantum-safe schemes: the Kyber (ML-KEM) and FrodoKEM key encapsulation mechanisms, and the Dilithium (ML-DSA) and Falcon (FN-DSA) signature schemes. We also develop the mathematical background on lattices needed to understand why Kyber, FrodoKEM, Dilithium and Falcon are regarded as lattice-based cryptosystems, and we provide insight into the computational hardness of the underlying lattice problems. The exposition is intended to be accessible to senior undergraduate students and beginning graduate students.

                                      Abstract
      We present four quantum-safe schemes: the Kyber (ML-KEM) and FrodoKEM
  key encapsulation mechanisms, and the Dilithium (ML-DSA) and Falcon (FN-DSA)
  signature schemes. We also develop the mathematical background on lattices needed
  to understand why Kyber, FrodoKEM, Dilithium and Falcon are regarded as lattice-
  based cryptosystems, and we provide insight into the computational hardness of the
  underlying lattice problems. The exposition is intended to be accessible to senior
  undergraduate students and beginning graduate students, and closely follows the
  accompanying video lecture series PQC Explained, Kyber and Dilithium, The Math-
  ematics of Lattice-Based Cryptography, and The LLL Algorithm, which are available
  at the website cryptography101.ca.

§1 Introduction                                                                        1


1    Introduction
In August 2024, the U.S. government’s National Institute of Standards and Technology
(NIST) published a suite of standards for a key encapsulation mechanism and for digi-
tal signature schemes designed to be resistant to attacks by quantum computers. These
quantum-safe schemes are intended to replace widely deployed RSA and elliptic curve
cryptography (ECC), both of which are vulnerable to quantum computing attacks. Al-
though the timeline for the development of cryptographically relevant quantum com-
puters remains uncertain, efforts to transition from RSA and ECC to quantum-safe alter-
natives are rapidly gaining momentum.
     Among the quantum-safe cryptographic schemes standardized by NIST, the key en-
capsulation mechanism Kyber and the digital signature scheme Dilithium are expected
to see the broadest deployment in the near future. The security of Kyber relies on the
presumed hardness of the Module Learning With Errors (MLWE) problem, whereas the
security of Dilithium is based on both the MLWE problem and the Module Short Integer
Solution (MSIS) problem. These problems are the module variants of the well-studied
Learning With Errors (LWE) and Short Integer Solution (SIS) problems, respectively.
     These notes give detailed descriptions and analyses of Kyber and Dilithium. We
show how the SIS and LWE problems—together with their module variants, MSIS and
MLWE—can be cast as computational problems on lattices, justifying the classification
of Kyber and Dilithium as lattice-based cryptosystems. We also describe FrodoKEM, a
key encapsulation mechanism built on the unstructured LWE problem and standardized
by the International Organization for Standardization (ISO), and Falcon, an SIS-based
signature scheme over NTRU lattices currently undergoing standardization by NIST.

Organization. The remainder of this document is organized as follows. In §2, we give
an introduction to the theory of lattices and define fundamental computational lattice
problems: the Shortest Vector Problem (SVP), the Shortest Independent Vectors Problem
(SIVP), the Closest Vector Problem (CVP), and their approximate versions, approx-SVP,
approx-SIVP, and approx-CVP. In §3 and §4, we show how SIS and LWE can be for-
mulated as lattice problems, and explain their connections to SVP and SIVP. The mod-
ule variants of SIS and LWE are introduced in §5. Detailed descriptions of Kyber and
Dilithium are provided in §6 and §7, Falcon is introduced in §8, and FrodoKEM is de-
scribed in §9. The lattice problems SIS, LWE, MSIS, and MLWE can be tackled using
the LLL and BKZ lattice basis reduction algorithms described in §10 and §11. The per-
formance of LLL and BKZ plays a central role in assessing the hardness of the lattice
problems and in motivating the parameter choices used in Kyber, Dilithium and Falcon.
Six applications of the LLL algorithm are presented in §12: solving short-secret LWE,
solving SIS, finding integer relations, performing simultaneous Diophantine approxi-
mation, mounting a side-channel attack on the ECDSA signature scheme, and finding
small roots of univariate polynomials modulo a composite integer with unknown fac-
torization. In §13, we describe the Number-Theoretic Transform (NTT), a fast algorithm
for polynomial multiplication that is essential for efficient implementation of Kyber and

    Readers are encouraged to attempt some of the exercises at the end of each section
(without relying on LLMs!). Computational exercises can be completed using a computer
algebra system such as SageMath, Maple, or Mathematica. Answers to the computational
problems are provided in Appendix B.

Advanced study. The research literature on lattices is vast and broad. While these
notes offer a solid introduction to lattice-based cryptography, they lack coverage in cer-
tain areas, such as worst-case to average-case reductions, security proofs, and protocols
with advanced functionalities. There are many possible research directions depending
on whether your interests lie in the underlying mathematics, protocol design and anal-
ysis, implementation, theory, or applications. Once you have identified a topic that you
find especially interesting, you could select a few foundational papers on that topic and
read them carefully. For instance, if you are interested in lattice basis reduction, you
could read the original LLL paper; if you are interested in KEMs, you could read the
paper that first described Kyber. To find topics and papers of interest, you can consult
the “Notes and further references” section, browse abstracts on the IACR ePrint Archive
(https://eprint.iacr.org), or ask your advisor for suggestions. You may find many of the
latest research papers difficult to read initially, but as your knowledge grows, grasping
their main ideas will become much easier.

1.1   Notes and further references
The video series Post-Quantum Cryptography Explained (https://cryptography101.ca/pqc)
provides an elementary introduction to post-quantum cryptography and lattice-based
cryptography.
     Lattices are fundamental structures that play a central role in numerous areas of
mathematics and computer science, including the geometry of numbers, coding the-
ory, optimization, and cryptography. The geometry of numbers is a branch of number
theory that applies geometric techniques, particularly those involving lattices, to prob-
lems concerning integers and algebraic numbers. The subject was founded by Hermann
Minkowski in the late nineteenth century; a classical reference is the book by Cassels
[48]. Notable applications of lattices include H. Lenstra’s polynomial-time algorithm
[136] for integer linear programming in fixed dimension n, Viazovska’s solution [200]
of the sphere packing problem in dimension 8, the work of Kannan and Lovász [119] on
the covering radius of convex bodies, and the capacity-achieving lattice coding scheme
for the additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) channel developed by Erez and Zamir
[78]. More recently, in 2023, Reis and Rothvoss [185] introduced a (log(2n)) O (n) -time
randomized algorithm for solving integer programs in n variables.
     Kyber and Dilithium were standardized by NIST in August 2024 as ML-KEM (FIPS 203)
[159] and ML-DSA (FIPS 204) [158], respectively, whereas Falcon is being standardized as
FN-DSA in FIPS 206, which at the time of writing has not yet been finalized. FrodoKEM
was standardized by ISO in June 2026 [117]. These notes focus on developing a thorough
understanding of Kyber, Dilithium and FrodoKEM, and providing background informa-
tion to appreciate Falcon. As part of its post-quantum cryptography standardization ini-
tiative, NIST has also finalized standards for the stateful hash-based signature schemes
LMS and XMSS in SP 800-208 [157], as well as the stateless hash-based signature scheme
SPHINCS+ in FIPS 205 [160]. Menezes [149] gives an overview of these schemes.

The sets of natural numbers, integers, rational numbers, real numbers, and complex
numbers are denoted by N, Z, Q, R, and C, respectively. We write Rn for the n-dimensional

The length of such a vector x is kx k = x 12 + x 22 + · · · + x n2 , which is also denoted kx k2

    Informally, a lattice can be viewed as a regular, repeating arrangement of points in
real space. Formally, lattices are defined as follows.

Definition 2.1 A lattice L in Rn is the set of all integer linear combinations of m lin-

[b1 , b2 , . . . , bm ] is called a basis of L and we write L = L(B). The dimension of L is n, and
the rank of L is m.
      The lattice L consists of all vectors of the form

where the scalars c i are integers. The basis B can be represented by an n ×m basis matrix,
also denoted by B, whose columns are the basis vectors b1 , b2 , . . . , bm :

With this notation, the lattice can be described compactly as L = {Bx : x ∈ Zm }.

Definition 2.2 A lattice L is a discrete additive subgroup of Rn .
§2.2 Examples                                                                                     5


    Here, L being an additive subgroup of Rn means that L is a non-empty subset of Rn
that is closed under vector addition and subtraction; that is, x +y, −x ∈ L for all x, y ∈ L.
The term discrete means that there exists an ε > 0 such that, for every x ∈ L, there are
no other lattice points within distance ε of x. We omit the proof that Definitions 2.1 and
2.2 are equivalent.
    In cryptographic applications, one typically works with lattices whose basis vectors
have integer coordinates, that is, b1 , b2 , . . . , bm ∈ Zn . In this case, L ⊆ Zn and L is
called an integer lattice. The lattices considered in the remainder of this document will
primarily be integer lattices.

Definition 2.3 A full-rank lattice in Rn is a lattice of rank n.
      If L is a full-rank lattice in Rn with basis B = [b1 , b2 , . . . , bn ], then B is also a ba-
sis of the vector space Rn . The lattice L consists of all integer linear combinations of
b1 , b2 , . . . , bn , whereas the vector space Rn consists of all real linear combinations of
these same vectors.

Definition 2.4 Let L and L 0 be lattices in Rn . Then L 0 is a sublattice of L if L 0 ⊆ L.
      To show that L 0 is a sublattice of L, it suffices to verify that each vector b 0 in a basis
B 0 of L 0 is an element of L, that is, can be expressed as an integer linear combination of
the vectors in a basis B of L.
    Henceforth, unless explicitly stated otherwise, all lattices and sublattices will be as-
sumed to be full-rank integer lattices.

    Figures 2.1(b) and 2.1(c) suggest that L 2 and L 3 are in fact the same lattice. This can
be confirmed by verifying that each lattice is a sublattice of the other. Indeed, L 2 ⊆ L 3
since

     The basis B 2 = [(2, 0), (0, 1)] for lattice L 2 is “nicer” than the basis B 3 = [(−2, −2), (4, 3)],
since the vectors in B 2 are shorter and mutually orthogonal. In general, the difficulty of
computational problems on lattices depends heavily on the quality of the basis used to
represent the lattice. For example, consider the Shortest Vector Problem (SVP), which
asks for a shortest nonzero vector in a lattice, given a basis for the lattice. Examining the
basis B 2 immediately reveals that (0, 1) is a shortest nonzero vector of L 2 . In contrast,
if L 2 were presented using the basis B 3 , then identifying such a vector would be signif-
icantly less straightforward. For another illustration of the benefits of a “good” lattice
basis, see Example 2.24.
     A common approach to solving lattice problems is therefore to first find a good basis
for the lattice in question, meaning one whose vectors are relatively short and nearly
orthogonal. The most well-known algorithm for this task is the LLL algorithm, which is
described in §10.

2.3    Bases of a lattice
Let L = L(B) be an n-dimensional lattice in Rn with ordered basis B = [b1 , b2 , . . . , bn ].
The following operations transform B into another basis for the same lattice:

   (i) Exchange two basis vectors: bi ↔ b j .

  (ii) Replace a basis vector by its negation: bi ← −bi .

 (iii) Add an integer multiple of one basis vector to another: bi ← bi + cb j where c ∈ Z.

Each of these corresponds to an elementary column operation on the basis matrix B. The
first two operations change the sign of the determinant of B, while the third operation
leaves the determinant unchanged.
     By repeatedly applying these operations, one obtains infinitely many distinct bases
for the same lattice. The following theorem characterizes all bases of a lattice.

Theorem 2.9 (characterization of lattice bases) Let L = L(B 1 ) be an n-dimensional lat-

   The volume1 of a lattice provides a quantitative measure of how densely the lattice
points are distributed in space: larger volumes correspond to sparser lattices. If L is
two-dimensional, then its volume coincides with the area of any of its parallelepipeds.

Definition 2.11 The volume of a lattice L = L(B) is defined as vol(L) = | det(B)|.

2.5     Fundamental lattice problems
We now introduce several fundamental computational problems on lattices whose pre-
sumed hardness underpins the security of lattice-based cryptosystems. Throughout, a
lattice L is specified by a basis B, and all lattices are assumed to be full-rank integer
lattices of dimension n.

2.5.1    Shortest Vector Problem (SVP)
Definition 2.17 The Shortest Vector Problem (SVP) is defined as follows: given a lattice
L = L(B), find a nonzero lattice vector of smallest length λ 1 (L).
     SVP has been shown to be NP-hard, and it is therefore reasonable to assume that it
is hard in the worst case. The fastest classical algorithm known for SVP runs in (heuris-
tic) time 20.292n+o (n) , whereas the best quantum algorithm known is slightly faster, with
(heuristic) running time 20.256n+o (n) . In both cases, the running time is fully exponential
in the lattice dimension.
     A natural relaxation of SVP is the approximate version, in which one seeks a nonzero
lattice vector whose length is within a prescribed approximation factor of λ 1 (L).

Definition 2.18 The Approximate Shortest Vector Problem (approx-SVP or SVPγ ) is de-
fined as follows: given a lattice L = L(B), find a nonzero lattice vector of length at most
γ · λ 1 (L), where γ is the approximation factor.
    Notice that SVP1 coincides with SVP. As γ increases, SVPγ becomes easier; more
precisely, if γ 1 ≥ γ 2 then SVPγ1 ≤ SVPγ2 3 . For constant approximation factors γ , SVPγ
                                                                              √
remains NP-hard. However, SVPγ is unlikely to be NP-hard when γ > n. For approxi-
mation factor γ = 2k , the fastest classical algorithm known for SVPγ runs in time 2Θ̃(n/k ) ,
where the Θ̃ notation suppresses a power of log n. When the approximation factor is very
large, more precisely when γ > 2 (n log log n)/ log n , SVPγ can be solved in polynomial time

2.5.2   Shortest Independent Vectors Problem (SIVP)
Another important lattice problem is to find many short linearly independent lattice
vectors.

Definition 2.19 The Shortest Independent Vectors Problem (SIVP) is defined as follows:
given a lattice L = L(B), find n linearly independent lattice vectors, each of length at
most λn (L).

Definition 2.20 The Approximate Shortest Independent Vectors Problem (approx-SIVP or
SIVPγ ) is defined as follows: given a lattice L = L(B), find n linearly independent lattice
vectors, each of length at most γ · λn (L).
    It is worth emphasizing that a solution to SIVP need not form a lattice basis; the
vectors obtained might be linearly independent without spanning the full lattice (see
Exercises 2.18 and 2.19).
    The complexity status of SIVP and approx-SIVP closely parallels that of SVP and
approx-SVP. In particular, SIVP is NP-hard, as is SIVPγ for constant approximation fac-
tors γ , and the fastest algorithms for these problems have fully exponential running time.
Moreover, there is a known reduction SIVPγ √n ≤ SVPγ , further highlighting the close
relationship between these fundamental lattice problems.

2.6     Notes and further references
The first monograph devoted to algorithmic problems in lattices and their computational
complexity is the 2002 book by Micciancio and Goldwasser [152]. Part IV of Galbraith’s
book [87] introduces lattices and explores their applications in cryptanalysis. Nguyen
[163] explains the connections between the Hermite constants, lattice algorithms, and
sphere packings. Peikert [177] provides a comprehensive survey of the major develop-
ments in lattice-based cryptography up to 2015, including fully homomorphic encryption
(FHE) and attribute-based encryption (ABE). More recently, Lyubashevsky [144] offers
a detailed exposition of the mathematical foundations and design principles underlying
§2.6 Notes and further references                                                          16


SIS- and LWE-based cryptosystems, including Kyber and Dilithium. Kyber and Dilithium
are fully specified in the NIST standards FIPS 203 [159] and FIPS 204 [158].
     Conway and Sloane’s book [58] is a rich source of information on the Leech lattice
Λ24 . The basis matrix for Λ24 presented in Example 2.13 is taken from Figure 4.12 of
that book. Bonnecaze and Solé [37] gave a construction of the Leech lattice from the
binary (23, 12, 7)-Golay code. The sphere packing problem is to find an arrangement of
non-overlapping unit balls in Rn so that the proportion of space they cover is as large as
possible. Cohn, Kumar, Miller, Radchenko and Viazovska [57] proved that the densest
sphere packing in R24 is attained with unit balls centered at the points of the Leech
lattice. This work builds on Viazovska’s proof [200] that the densest√sphere packing in
R8 is attained by placing unit balls at the points of the scaled lattice 2E 8 (the E 8 lattice
is defined in Exercise 10.11).
     In 1998, Ajtai [4] proved that SVP is NP-hard under randomized reductions. Recently,
in 2026, Wan [201] removed the randomness from Ajtai’s reduction, finally establishing
the NP-hardness of SVP. Khot [120] proved that the approximate version SVPγ remains
NP-hard under randomized reductions for constant approximation factors γ . The claim
                                              √
that SVPγ is unlikely to be NP-hard for γ > n is supported by a result of Aharonov and
Regev [2] that there exists c > 0 for which GapSVPc √n lies in NP ∩ coNP (GapSVPβ is a
decisional version of SVP). Blömer and Seifert [32] proved that SIVPγ is NP-hard for con-
stant approximation factors γ . Laarhoven, van de Pol and de Weger [127] and Stephens-
Davidowitz [196] provide comprehensive overviews of the relationships between the
main lattice problems. Stephens-Davidowitz [196] gave a proof that SIVPγ √n ≤ SVPγ
for every γ ≥ 1.
     Micciancio [150] gave an elementary proof that CVP is NP-hard. Micciancio [151]
gave polynomial-time reductions CVP ≤ SIVP and SIVPγ ≤ CVPγ for every γ ≥ 1. In
2026, an internal OpenAI model [175] proved that CVPn 1/400 is NP-hard; this was the first
unconditional NP-hardness result for SVPγ , SIVPγ or CVPγ with a polynomial approx-
imation factor γ = nc (with constant c > 0). Goldreich, Micciancio, Safra and Seifert
[98] showed that for any γ ≥ 1, SVPγ polynomial-time reduces to CVPγ . Conversely,
Stephens-Davidowitz [196] proved that CVPγ 2 √n polynomial-time reduces to SVPγ .
     Babai [19] introduced two conceptually simple polynomial-time algorithms for CVPγ .
His nearest plane algorithm achieves an approximation factor of γ = 2n/2 , while his
rounding algorithm (see Exercise 12.5) attains γ = 1 + 2n( 92 ) n/2 . The nearest plane algo-
rithm has found applications in several areas beyond cryptography. In particular, Chen
et al. [51] showed in 2025 that GPTQ, a widely used method for quantizing the weights
of large language models (LLMs), can be viewed as an application of the nearest plane
algorithm.
     Gao [90] constructed a family of lattices for which the Bounded Distance Decoding
(BDD) problem (Definition 4.19) is NP-hard but solvable in polynomial time on aver-
age, demonstrating that worst-case NP-hardness of a lattice problem does not imply its
average-case hardness.

    The security of the Dilithium signature scheme relies on the assumed hardness of
the Short Integer Solution (SIS) problem. This section introduces SIS, presents a lattice
formulation of SIS, and explores its relationship with SVP and SIVP.

3.1    Problem statement
Notation. q is a prime; Zq = {0, 1, 2, . . . , q −1} is the set of integers modulo q; Zm
                                                                                       q is the
set of length-m (column) vectors whose components are in Zq ; Zqn×m is the set of n × m
matrices whose entries are in Zq ; and [−B, B]m denotes the set of all length-m (column)
vectors whose components are integers in the interval [−B, B].
    The SIS problem was introduced by Miklós Ajtai in 1996. It is parameterized by
four values: positive integers n and m with n  m, a prime modulus q, and a bound B
satisfying B  q/2 and Bm  qn .

Definition 3.1 The Short Integer Solution problem, denoted SIS(n, m, q, B), is defined as
follows. Given a uniformly random matrix A ∈R Zqn×m , find a nonzero vector z ∈ Zm
such that Az = 0 (mod q) and z ∈ [−B, B]m ; see Figure 3.1.




                                    Figure 3.1: SIS problem.

     SIS seeks to find a small nonzero solution in the null space of A (mod q). While
Gaussian elimination can efficiently determine a basis for this null space, the challenge
is to find a nonzero element all of whose coordinates lie within [−B, B].
     When n ≥ m, one expects that A has rank m, meaning that z = 0 is the only solution
to Az = 0 (mod q), and thus no SIS solution exists. This explains the requirement that
n  m, which also ensures that A has full rank over Zq with overwhelming probability.
Throughout the remainder of this section, we therefore assume that A has rank n.
§3.1 Problem statement                                                                             21


    Because Bm > qn , the pigeonhole principle guarantees the existence of two distinct
vectors z 1 , z 2 ∈ [−B/2, B/2]m such that Az 1 = Az 2 (mod q). Consequently, their differ-
ence z = z 1 − z 2 yields a solution to the SIS problem, establishing that a solution must
exist. It is important to note, however, that an SIS solution is not unique. Indeed, if z is
one SIS solution, then so is −z.

3.3.2   Average-case hardness of SIS
It is natural to conjecture that SIS is hard in the worst case. However, in cryptographic
applications an SIS instance is generated by choosing a matrix A uniformly at random.
Therefore, what is required is not merely worst-case hardness, but rather the guarantee
that SIS is always hard, except with negligible probability. In other words, we need SIS
to be hard on average.
     Another concern with SIS is that the corresponding approx-SVP instance has con-
siderable structure. In particular, the SIS lattice admits a basis matrix of the special form
given by (10), which is upper-triangular with q’s in the upper-left diagonal block and
1’s in the lower-right diagonal block. One might therefore be concerned that, even if
approx-SVP is hard in general, it could be significantly easier on the restricted family of
lattices arising from SIS instances.
§3.4 Notes and further references                                                        25


    In his seminal 1996 work, Ajtai alleviated these concerns by proving that SIS is hard
on average under standard complexity-theoretic assumptions. Specifically, he showed
that if approx-SIVP is hard in the worst case, then SIS is hard on average. Reductions
of this type are known as worst-case to average-case reductions, and they provide (con-
ditional) assurances for the average-case hardness of SIS since approx-SIVP is a natural
and well-studied lattice problem, at least for relatively small approximation factors.
    Ajtai’s reduction is technically involved and beyond the scope of this introductory
treatment. At a very high level (see Figure 3.2), the reduction starts from an arbitrary




                  Figure 3.2: Proving the average-case hardness of SIS.

n-dimensional lattice with basis D and efficiently generates a random SIS instance. A
solution to this SIS instance can then be efficiently transformed into a solution to approx-
SIVP in the lattice generated by D. Consequently, an efficient algorithm for solving SIS
on average would imply an efficient algorithm for solving approx-SIVP in the worst case.
    Ajtai’s worst-case to average-case reduction for SIS is one of the most remarkable
results in lattice-based cryptography. It should be noted, however, that the guarantee it
provides for the average-case hardness of SIS is asymptotic in nature. Furthermore, the
reduction is highly non-tight, which means that the algorithm that solves approx-SIVP
using an SIS solver is very inefficient. The asymptotic nature and non-tightness of the
reduction prevents it from being used directly to derive concrete parameters for practical
cryptographic schemes based on SIS.

3.4   Notes and further references
The SIS problem was introduced by Ajtai [3], who provided a worst-case to average-case
reduction from approx-SIVP to SIS. The approximation factor in Ajtai’s reduction was
later improved by Micciancio and Regev [154]. A proof of Theorem 3.9 can be found in
§1.6 of Stewart and Tall’s book [197].
    Gentry, Peikert and Vaikuntanathan (GPV) [92, 93] introduced a framework for con-
structing hash-and-sign signature schemes. This framework was later employed in the
§3.5 Exercises                                                                         26


design of the Falcon signature scheme by Fouque et al. [83]. Falcon (Fast-Fourier Lattice-
Based Compact Signatures over NTRU) derives its security from the hardness of SIS on
NTRU lattices. Falcon is currently undergoing standardization by NIST, with a draft
standard, FIPS 206, anticipated in 2026. The GPV framework and Falcon are introduced
in §8.
    Cash, Hofheinz, Kiltz and Peikert [47] introduced the concept of lattice-based bonsai
trees, using it to construct a stateless SIS-based signature scheme whose security proof
does not depend on the random oracle model.

     The security of a wide range of cryptographic protocols, including the Kyber key
encapsulation mechanism and the Dilithium signature scheme, relies on the hardness
of the Learning With Errors (LWE) problem. This section introduces LWE, presents a
lattice formulation of LWE, and explores its relationships with SVP and SIVP.

4.1    Problem statement
The LWE problem was introduced by Oded Regev in 2005. It is parameterized by four
values: positive integers m and n with m  n, a prime modulus q, and a noise bound B
satisfying B  q/2.

Definition 4.1 The Learning With Errors problem, denoted LWE(m, n, q, B), is defined
as follows. Choose a matrix A ∈R Zm×nq   , a secret vector s ∈R Zqn , and an error vector
e ∈R [−B, B] , and let b = As + e (mod q) ∈ Zm
             m
                                                  q . Given the pair (A, b), the goal is to
recover s; see Figure 4.1. The parameter m is the number of LWE samples.




                                   Figure 4.1: LWE problem.

    Observe that if B = 0, so that e = 0, then the problem is to solve the system of linear
equations As = b (mod q) for s. In this case, the set of all solutions can be efficiently
determined using Gaussian elimination over Zq . Hardness of LWE arises because of the
introduction of the noise e. We henceforth assume that B , 0.

Remark 4.2 (on the primality of q) The requirement that q be prime in Definition 4.1
is a matter of convenience rather than necessity. Its main effect is that Zq is a field, so
that Zqn is a vector space and the usual tools of linear algebra are available. For example,
§4.1 Problem statement                                                                 28


a uniformly random matrix A ∈ Zm×n  q   with m  n has rank n except with negligible
probability. As another example, the proof that LWE ≤ DLWE (Theorem 4.6) relies
on the primality of q. Similarly, a prime q is preferred in the MLWE setting of Kyber
and Dilithium (see §5), where the known security reductions are established for prime
moduli. The requirement is relaxed in §9, where the FrodoKEM scheme takes q to be a
power of two (215 or 216 ), which makes modular reduction particularly efficient.

Remark 4.3 (distribution choices in LWE) In Definition 4.1, the secret vector s is sam-
pled uniformly over Zqn and the error vector e uniformly from the range [−B, B]m . More
generally, s and e can be sampled from any distribution. For instance, discrete Gaus-
sian distributions are used in numerous cryptographic protocols including the Falcon
signature scheme (§8) and FrodoKEM (§9), and are central to establishing worst-case to
average-case security proofs. Alternatively, the centered binomial distribution is em-
ployed in Kyber; see §6.2. Furthermore, each coordinate of s and each coordinate of e
can be drawn from the same distribution, as is done in the short-secret variant of LWE
(Definition 4.7).
    The statement of the LWE problem implicitly assumes that the LWE solution s is
unique. In fact, the solution is expected to be unique with overwhelming probability
provided that the number m of rows of A is sufficiently greater than the number n of

4.4.4    Average-case hardness of LWE
As with SIS, it is reasonable to conjecture that LWE is hard in the worst case. However,
LWE instances are generated by selecting (A, s, e) uniformly at random. For crypto-
graphic applications, it is therefore crucial to establish average-case hardness, namely
that LWE is hard for random instances except with negligible probability.
    In his seminal 2005 work, Regev proved that LWE is hard on average, assuming that
approx-SIVP is quantum hard (i.e., intractable on quantum as well as classical comput-
ers) in the worst case. This worst-case to average-case reduction provides (conditional)
evidence for the average-case hardness of LWE, since it is reasonable to assume that
approx-SIVP is quantum hard in the worst case, at least for relatively small approxi-
mation factors. As with Ajtai’s reduction for SIS (§3.3.2), Regev’s result is asymptotic
and non-tight, and thus does not directly yield concrete parameter choices for practical
cryptosystems.

4.5     Notes and further references
The LWE problem was introduced by Regev [184], who gave a worst-case to average-case
quantum reduction from approx-SIVP to LWE. For a concrete analysis of the tightness
gap in Regev’s reduction, see the work of Chatterjee, Koblitz, Menezes and Sarkar [50].
    The Lindner-Peikert public-key encryption scheme [140] forms the basis for the Ky-
ber public-key encryption scheme specified in FIPS 203. LWE also forms the basis for a
wide variety of cryptographic protocols, including the identity-based encryption scheme
of Gentry, Peikert and Vaikuntanathan [92, 93], the hierarchical identity-based encryp-
tion scheme of Cash, Hofheinz, Kiltz and Peikert [47], the attribute-based encryption
scheme of Gorbunov, Vaikuntanathan and Wee [99], and the fully-homomorphic en-
cryption scheme of Cheon, Kim, Kim and Song [55].
    The embedding technique used in the primal attack on LWE described in §4.4.1
was originally introduced by Kannan [118] to reduce approx-CVP to SVP. Albrecht [8]
proposed a variant of the dual attack tailored to short-secret LWE. Howgrave-Graham
[114] introduced hybrid attacks, which combine lattice basis reduction with meet-in-the-
middle techniques.

    The method of transforming an LWE instance into a system of high-degree multi-
variate polynomial equations that can then be solved via linearization was introduced
by Arora and Ge [17]. Another known attack on LWE is the BKW attack introduced by
Blum, Kalai and Wasserman [33]. This attack has been refined by many authors, includ-
ing Kirchner and Fouque [122], Budroni, Guo, Johansson, Mårtensson and Wagner [44],
and Guo, Johansson, Mårtensson and Wagner [103]. However, none of these attacks are
effective against Kyber and Dilithium, as they require an impractically large number of
LWE samples. Machine learning-based approaches have also been investigated, most
recently by Alfarano, Saxena, Wenger, Charton and Lauter [11], although these methods
have so far achieved only limited success.

error term is replaced by deterministic rounding. Let integers q ≥ p ≥ 2 be fixed. Define
the rounding function b·cp : Zq → Zp by bxcp = b(p/q) · xc. This function naturally ex-

    The security of Kyber and Dilithium relies on the assumed hardness of the module
versions of the SIS and LWE problems. These variants are derived from SIS and LWE by

5.1    The polynomial ring Rq = Zq [x]/(x n + 1)
Let q be a prime and n a positive integer. The polynomial ring Rq = Zq [x]/(x n +1) is com-
posed of the polynomials in Zq [x] of degree less than n, with multiplication performed
using the reduction polynomial x n + 1.
      To multiply two polynomials f (x ), д(x ) ∈ Rq , one (i) multiplies them using ordinary
polynomial multiplication in Zq [x] to obtain a polynomial h(x ) ∈ Zq [x] of degree at most
2n − 2; and then (ii) divides h(x ) by x n + 1 to get a remainder polynomial r (x ) ∈ Zq [x]
of degree at most n − 1. The product of f (x ) and д(x ) in Rq is the remainder polynomial
r (x ).

5.4    Notes and further references
Ring-SIS, an analogue of SIS that employs certain polynomial rings, was formulated by
Lyubashevsky and Micciancio [145]. The module-based analogue, Module-SIS (MSIS),
which employs vectors of polynomials, was developed by Langlois and Stehlé [130].
    Ring-LWE, a variant of LWE that employs certain polynomial rings, was formulated
by Lyubashevsky, Peikert and Regev [146], who also provided a worst-case to average-
case quantum reduction from approx-SIVP in ideal lattices to Ring-LWE. The module
variant, Module-LWE (MLWE), was first introduced by Brakerski, Gentry and Vaikun-
tanathan [42], and a worst-case to average-case quantum reduction was developed by
Langlois and Stehlé [130]. A concrete analysis of the tightness gaps in the Ring-LWE and
MLWE reductions was carried out by Koblitz, Samajder, Sarkar and Singha [124], who
argued that the approximation factor in the SIVP problem is too large to yield meang-
ingful security guarantees in practice. Wenger et al. [202] provide concrete benchmarks
for several lattice-based attacks on LWE with parameter choices from Kyber and a Ring-
LWE-based homomorphic encryption scheme.

    Kyber-KEM is a quantum-safe key encapsulation mechanism (KEM) standardized by
NIST in FIPS 203, where its official name is Module-Lattice-based KEM (ML-KEM). It
is designed to offer strong security guarantees against attacks from both classical and
quantum computers. Kyber-KEM is based on the Kyber public-key encryption scheme
(Kyber-PKE), described next.

6.1    Kyber public-key encryption
The Kyber public-key encryption scheme can be viewed as a natural extension of the
Lindner-Peikert scheme described in §4.2, with elements in Zq replaced by polynomials
in the ring Rq = Zq [x]/(x n + 1).

Notation. Recall that Sη = { f ∈ Rq | k f k∞ ≤ η}, and that dxc denotes the near-
est integer to x with ties broken upward. The plaintext space is {0, 1}n . A plaintext
m = (m 0 , m 1 , . . . , mn−1 ) ∈ {0, 1}n is associated with the polynomial m(x ) = m 0 + m 1x +
· · · + mn−1x n−1 ∈ Rq . The rounding function Roundq (Definition 4.12) extends natu-
rally to polynomials in Rq by applying it coefficientwise. For instance, if q = 3329 then
Roundq (100 + 1000x + 2000x 2 + 3000x 3 ) = x + x 2 .
      The Kyber public-key encryption scheme without ciphertext compression is described
in Algorithm 6.1. The standardized version, which incorporates ciphertext compression,
is presented in §6.3. The three Kyber parameter sets specified in FIPS 203 are listed in
Table 6.1. Their intended security levels against classical attacks are approximately 128,
192 and 256 bits.

      larger public keys and ciphertexts.

6.4   Kyber-KEM
The official name of Kyber-KEM in FIPS 203 is Module-Lattice-based KEM (ML-KEM). As
shown in Algorithm 6.12, Kyber-KEM is derived by applying a variant of the Fujisaki-
Okamoto (FO) transform to the Kyber public-key encryption scheme. The FO trans-
form is a generic method for converting a public-key encryption scheme that is indistin-
guishable under chosen-plaintext attack to one that is indistinguishable under chosen-
ciphertext attack (Definition A.3).
    The transform utilizes three hash functions, G, H , and J , which are derived from
SHA3 and SHAKE256. Kyber-PKE is employed to encrypt a randomly chosen bit string
m of length 256. During encapsulation, derandomization is applied, whereby m and the
encapsulation key ek are hashed to produce a random seed R and the secret key K. The
random polynomial vectors r , e 1 and the random polynomial e 2 required for Kyber-PKE
are derived from R. This process transforms the randomized Kyber public-key encryption
scheme into a deterministic one, meaning the ciphertext c depends only on the message
m and encapsulation key ek, without relying on any additional random bits generated
during encryption.
    In decapsulation, the recipient decrypts the Kyber-PKE ciphertext c to recover m 0,
then hashes m 0 and ek to obtain R 0 and K 0. He then re-encrypts m 0 using R 0 and compares
the resulting ciphertext c 0 with the received c. If the encryption was performed correctly,
then m 0 will equal m with overwhelming probability and consequently R 0 = R and K 0 =
K. This ensures that the re-encryption of m results in the ciphertext c, which is why a
deterministic encryption scheme is necessary. However, if decryption fails and m 0 , m,
the re-encrypted ciphertext c 0 will differ from c with overwhelming probability.
    Therefore, if c 0 equals c, Bob accepts K as the shared key. Otherwise, he generates a
random key K obtained by hashing c and the secret z; in this case the decapsulation is
deemed to have failed.
    Kyber-KEM exhibits plaintext awareness, meaning that decapsulation will produce K
(and not K) only if the entity who performed the encapsulation knew K. This property is
designed to ensure resistance to chosen-ciphertext attacks because the adversary cannot
gain any useful information by submitting a ciphertext to Bob for decapsulation. Either
the adversary already knew K (in which case nothing new is learned when Bob returns
the same K), or the adversary does not know K, in which case Bob will almost certainly
§6.4 Kyber-KEM                                                                            64


return a key K that is randomly selected and independent of K, preventing the adversary
from learning anything useful.
    Decapsulation fails when c does not equal c 0, in which case the key K outputted
is different from the encapsulated key K. This failure can occur even if Alice and Bob
behave honestly, as there is a very small chance that a failure in the underlying Kyber-
PKE will cause m 0 to differ from m. However, for the domain parameters specified in
FIPS 203, the probability of Kyber-PKE decryption failure is negligible, and consequently
the probability of a Kyber-KEM failure is also extremely low.

for these parameter sets are approximately 128, 192 and 256 bits. Ideally, the decryption

     Decapsulation fails when at least one coefficient Ei of the error polynomial E(x ) =
eT r − sT e 1 + e 2 − sT eu + ev satisfies kEi k∞ > q/4. An adversary selects a random m,
computes the corresponding ciphertext c, and submits c to a decapsulation oracle. This
procedure is repeated until a decapsulation error occurs. Upon such a failure, the ad-

learned values r , e 1 , e 2 , eu and ev such that kE(x )k∞ > q/4.
     For the ML-KEM-768 parameter set, an adversary can make t = 264 queries to the
decapsulation oracle and expects to observe at least one failure with probability ε =
2−104 . In this setting, we have t/ε = 2168 which is below the target security level of
2192 . However, it is not known how to effectively exploit the information leaked by a
decapsulation failure to break the KEM, i.e., to distinguish between (K, C) and (K, C)
where (K, C) is a valid key-ciphertext pair and K is an independently generated random
key.
     Some strategies have been proposed to increase the probability of decapsulation fail-
ure. For example, an adversary might repeatedly sample random m until the correspond-
ing values r and e 1 have unusually large norms, thereby increasing the likelihood of fail-
ure. However, no such strategies are currently known to be effective in breaking Kyber-
KEM, especially when the number of decapsulation queries is limited to 264 , which is a
realistic upper bound in practice.

Security. Kyber-KEM has been proven to be indistinguishable under chosen-ciphertext
attack (Definition A.5) assuming that D-MLWE is intractable, and that G, H , and J are
modelled as random oracles. Kyber-KEM has also been proven indistinguishable under
chosen-ciphertext attack by a quantum adversary, who is permitted to make queries to
G, H and J in quantum superposition.

6.5   Notes and further references
Kyber-PKE was developed by Bos et al. [41]. The Fujisaki-Okamoto transform was in-
troduced in 1999 [86]. A variant of it, due to Hofheinz, Hövelmanns and Kiltz [111], was
used by Bos et al. [41] in the design of Kyber-KEM. For a comprehensive description of
Kyber-KEM, including the specifications of the hash functions G, H , and J , the eXtend-
able Output Function (XOF) used to generate A, and the pseudorandom function (PRF)
used to generate s, e, r , e 1 and e 2 , see FIPS 203 [159]. Examples of Kyber-KEM for the
three standardized parameter sets can be found at the CrypTool-Online website [63].
    D’Anvers et al. [64] showed how information leaked through Kyber-KEM decapsula-
tion failure can be exploited to formulate an MLWE instance with a secret that is smaller
than the original pair (s, e), thereby making the problem easier to solve. They then ap-
plied standard cost estimates for solving MLWE to approximate the time required to
recover the secret key. Their analysis indicates that the attack is ineffective when the
§6.5 Notes and further references                                                                66


number of decapsulation queries is limited to 264 . In subsequent work, D’Anvers, Rossi
and Virdia [66] proposed a technique called directional failure boosting, in which a pre-
viously identified failing ciphertext is leveraged to dramatically accelerate the discovery
of additional ciphertexts that also fail decapsulation.
     Side-channel attacks against Kyber implementations continue to be an active area of
research. A comprehensive survey on side-channel attacks on Kyber implementations
was presented in 2024 by Ravi, Chattopadhyay, D’Anvers and Baksi [183]. Recent notable
contributions include the works of Hermelink, Ning, Petri and Strieder [107], Bernstein
et al. [30], and Fouque, Marion, Nguyen and Wallet [85].
     The security of Kyber and Dilithium rests on the hardness of problems in struc-
tured lattices: as explained in §5, the lattices underlying the Module-LWE and Module-
SIS problems possess considerable structure in that their basis matrices consist of anti-
circulant blocks. FrodoKEM, the key encapsulation mechanism described in §9, takes a
different approach, basing its security on the hardness of LWE in unstructured lattices.
The absence of algebraic structure in FrodoKEM’s lattices affords a more conservative
security guarantee than that of Kyber, but comes at the considerable cost of larger public
keys and ciphertexts, and slower encryption and decryption.
     Most PQC deployments adopt a hybrid approach. In this model, traditional elliptic-
curve key agreement such as elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH) is combined with a
quantum-resistant key establishment mechanism such as Kyber-KEM. The final shared
secret key is derived by combining the outputs of both schemes via a key derivation func-
tion. Hybrid constructions mitigate harvest-now, decrypt-later attacks by ensuring that
recorded traffic remains secure even if large-scale quantum computers become available
in the future. At the same time, the inclusion of a classical and well-studied primitive
such as ECDH provides a hedge against the possibility that unforeseen weaknesses are
later discovered in the quantum-resistant component. This dual protection, however, is
lost if cryptographically relevant quantum computers become available and major weak-
nesses are discovered in the quantum-resistant scheme.
     Giacon, Heuer and Poettering [95] studied key combiners for hybrid key agreement
that remain secure provided that at least one of the constituent KEMs is secure. NIST’s
SP 800-227 [161] recommends the following generic key combiner. For i ∈ {1, 2}, let eki ,
c i and Ki denote the encapsulation key, ciphertext and shared secret key for two KEMs.
The combined key is then computed as K = H (K 1 , K 2 , c 1 , c 2 , ek 1 , ek 2 , domain_sep), where
“domain_sep” is a string that uniquely identifies the composite KEM scheme in use. A
hybrid KEM tailored to combine X25519 elliptic curve key agreement with ML-KEM-
768 was proposed by Barbosa et al. [24]; this construction achieves improved efficiency
compared to generic combiners.

     Dilithium is a quantum-safe signature scheme standardized by NIST in FIPS 204,
where it is officially called the Module-Lattice-based Digital Signature Algorithm (ML-
DSA). It is designed to provide strong security guarantees against attacks from both
classical and quantum computers. In §7.1, we introduce a “toy” version of Dilithium to
illustrate the main ideas underlying the scheme. We then examine several weaknesses
of this simplified scheme and address them in §7.2. Finally, we incorporate public key
compression in §7.3 to obtain the full version of Dilithium.

7.1     Dilithium (toy version)
The design of Dilithium is inspired by the Schnorr signature scheme, which we briefly
recall next.

7.1.1       Schnorr signature scheme
Let д be a generator of a cyclic group G of prime order n, and let H be a hash function.
Alice’s secret signing key is an integer a ∈R [1, n − 1], and her corresponding public ver-
ification key is the group element A = дa . Observe that recovering a from A is precisely
the discrete logarithm problem in G.
     To sign a message M ∈ {0, 1}∗ , Alice first selects an integer y ∈R [1, n − 1] and
then computes w = дy , c = H (M kw ), and z = y + ca mod n. The value w is called the
commitment, c is the challenge, and z is the response. Alice’s signature on M is the pair
σ = (c, z). To verify a purported signature, Bob uses Alice’s public key A to compute
w 0 = дz A−c , and accepts the signature if and only if c = H (M kw 0 ).
     Correctness follows by observing that

            z ≡ y + ca (mod n) ⇔ дz = дy+ca ⇔ дy = дz (дa ) −c ⇔ w = дz A−c .

Therefore w 0 = w, so Bob and Alice compute the same challenge value.

7.1.4   Five limitations and their solutions
Next, we examine five issues with the toy version of Dilithium and modifications that
address them.

Issue #1: Large public keys. For the ML-DSA-87 parameters, the matrix A ∈ Rqk×` has
size 41,216 bytes, and the vector t ∈ Rqk has size 5,888 bytes, so the public key (A, t ) has
size 47,104 bytes. To reduce this, A is generated from a randomly selected 256-bit seed ρ,
and its entries are derived from ρ using a publicly known pseudorandom bit generator
called ExpandA. The updated public key, (ρ, t ), has size 5,920 bytes.
    FIPS 204 also specifies a method for compressing t, reducing its size from 5,888 bytes
to 2,560 bytes, further reducing the public key size to 2,592 bytes.

7.2.3    Security
If the short-secret D-MLWE problem (Definition 5.18) is intractable, an adversary cannot
derive any information about the secret key component s 1 (or s 2 ) from the public key
(ρ, t ). Evaluating the difficulty of signature forgery is more complex. To simplify the
analysis, we will make a few simplifications to the signature scheme and provide an
informal argument that a forger with access to the public key (ρ, t ) cannot produce a
valid signed message.
     The forger’s task is as follows: given the verification key (ρ, t ), find a message M
and signature (c̃, z) such that kzk∞ < γ 1 − β and c̃ = H (µ kw 1 ), where µ = H (M ), w 1 =
HighBits0 (Az − ct, 2γ 2 ), and c = SampleInBall(c̃). It is important to note that c depends
on c̃, c̃ depends on w 1 , and w 1 depends on c, creating a circular dependency. Assuming
that H has no weaknesses, it would appear that the forger’s best strategy is to randomly
select M and w 1 ∈ Rqk , where each coefficient in w 1 is in the range [0, (q − 1)/(2γ 2 )], and
then compute µ = H (M ), c̃ = H (µ kw 1 ), and c = SampleInBall(c̃). The remaining task is
to find a z that satisfies the signature conditions.

7.3.4    Security
Compressing the public key component t has no impact on the security of Dilithium.
In particular, the full scheme has been proven existentially unforgeable under chosen-
message attacks (Definition A.7), assuming the hardness of the D-MLWE and MSIS prob-
lems, and modelling H as a random oracle.

Remark 7.10 (selecting Dilithium parameters) The ML-DSA-44, ML-DSA-65 and ML-
DSA-87 parameter sets specified in FIPS 204 (see Table 7.1) were carefully engineered to
optimize the trade-offs between security, public key size, signature size, implementation
efficiency, and the expected number of iterations during signature generation. The fol-
lowing notes illustrate the delicate balance required when selecting the parameters q, n,
k, `, η, γ 1 , γ 2 , τ , β, d and ω.
   1. To facilitate fast polynomial multiplication in Rq via the Number-Theoretic Trans-
      form (see §13.3), the degree n was chosen to be a power of two, and the prime q
      was chosen to satisfy the condition q ≡ 1 (mod 2n).
   2. The dimensions k and ` can be increased to achieve higher security levels against
      MLWE and MSIS attacks without altering the underlying polynomial ring Rq .
      However, increasing k makes the public key larger (since t 1 ∈ Rqk ), while increasing
      ` makes the signature larger (since z ∈ Rq` ).
   3. Minimizing γ 1 and γ 2 is desirable to maximize resistance to MSIS attacks; cf. equa-
      tion (37). Conversely, larger values for γ 1 and γ 2 are preferred because they in-
      crease the acceptance probabilities p1 and p2 (see equations (40) and (42)), thereby
      reducing the expected number of iterations during signature generation.
   4. A larger secret bound η enhances resistance against MLWE attacks, but it conse-
      quently increases β (since β = τη), which lowers the acceptance probabilities p1
      and p2 .
   5. While a smaller value of τ is desirable because
                                                  it reduces β, τ must remain suf-
      ficiently large to ensure that the size 2τ 256
                                                  τ  of the challenge space Bτ provides
      adequate security.
   6. Increasing the compression parameter d reduces the size of the public key compo-
      nent t 1 , and decreasing ω reduces the size of the hint vector h. However, choosing
      a large d or a small ω reduces the acceptance probability p3 (see equation (43)),
      which increases the expected number of iterations.

7.4     Notes and further references
Dilithium’s design follows the Fiat-Shamir methodology [80] which is a generic method
for converting a three-move interactive identification scheme into a non-interactive sig-
nature scheme by hashing the message and the prover’s commitment together to gen-
erate the challenge. Dilithium was designed by Ducas, Kiltz, Lepoint, Lyubashevsky,
§7.4 Notes and further references                                                   86


Schwabe and Seiler [72] and draws on ideas from several earlier works, most notably the
papers of Lyubashevsky [142, 143] and Bai and Galbraith [20]. It was heavily optimized
to reduce public-key and signature sizes, while ensuring fast and constant-time imple-
mentations. For a full description of Dilithium, including specifications of ExpandA,
ExpandS, ExpandMask, H , and SampleInBall, see FIPS 204 [158]. Formal security proofs
for Dilithium follow a reductionist approach, building on the “Fiat-Shamir with aborts
paradigm” originally proposed by Lyubashevsky [142]. These proofs are notably com-
plex; detailed analyses were presented by Barbosa et al. [23] and Devevey et al. [69].
    Azevedo-Oliveira, Calle Viera, Cogliati and Goubin [18] developed a practical linear-
programming method that recovers the private key component t 0 from a Dilithium public
key (ρ, t 1 ) together with a collection of signed messages. Approximately 200,000 signa-
tures were needed for the ML-DSA-44 parameter set, while about 500,000 signatures were
required for the ML-DSA-65 and ML-DSA-87 parameter sets. These results support the
statement in the FIPS 204 document that “The low-order bits of t can be reconstructed
from a small number of signatures and, therefore, need not be regarded as secret.”
    The vulnerability of Dilithium implementations to side-channel attacks remains an
active area of research. A comprehensive survey of such attacks was presented in 2024 by
Ravi, Chattopadhyay, D’Anvers and Baksi [183]. Recent notable works include attacks
exploiting potential information leakage arising from rejection sampling by Zhou, Wang,
Sun and Yu [208] and by Liu, Wang, Wei, Ding, Zhang, Liu and Zhu [141], as well as fault
attacks studied by Ulitzsch, Marzougui, Bagia, Tibouchi and Seifert [198], Krahmer, Pessl,
Land and Güneysu [126], and Kosuge and Xagawa [125].
    Threshold signature schemes distribute a secret signing key among multiple parties
so that a valid signature can only be produced by a coalition of parties exceeding a given
size threshold. In 2026, multi-party computation techniques were used by Bienstock,
de Castro, Escudero, Polychroniadou and Takahashi [31], and by Celi, del Pino, Espitau,
Niot and Prest [49], to construct threshold signing protocols for Dilithium.
    Another prominent lattice-based signature scheme that follows the Fiat-Shamir method-
ology is BLISS (Bimodal Lattice Signature Scheme), designed by Ducas, Durmus, Le-
point and Lyubashevsky [70]. A primary difference between BLISS and Dilithium is
their choices of distributions for the per-message secret y and the signature component
z. BLISS selects y from a discrete Gaussian distribution and uses rejection sampling to
ensure that z follows a bimodal discrete Gaussian distribution that is independent of
the signing key. In contrast, Dilithium selects y from a uniform distribution and uses
rejection sampling to ensure that z follows a distribution that is independent of the
signing key component s 1 and has coefficients bounded in the infinity norm. Conse-
quently, BLISS has smaller public keys and signatures than Dilithium at the same se-
curity level. However, BLISS’s Gaussian sampling and rejection sampling have been
shown to be highly vulnerable to side-channel attacks. Specifically, Groot Bruinderink,
Hülsing, Lange and Yarom [101] presented a key-recovery cache timing attack that tar-
gets the Gaussian sampler, and Espitau, Fouque, Gérard and Tibouchi [79] presented a
key-recovery electromagnetic radiation attack that targets the rejection sampling. Mar-
zougui, Wisiol, Gersch, Krämer and Seifert [147] devised power analysis attacks on

     Falcon is a lattice-based quantum-safe signature scheme that was selected by NIST
for standardization in July 2022. Falcon is expected to be published as FIPS 206, with
a draft to be released in 2026 and the final standard expected in 2027. NIST’s official
name for Falcon is Fast-Fourier Transform over NTRU-Lattice-Based Digital Signature
Algorithm (FN-DSA). Falcon’s principal advantage over Dilithium lies in its significantly
smaller public keys and signatures. However, it introduces unique implementation chal-
lenges. Signature generation relies heavily on intricate floating-point arithmetic, and
achieving constant-time execution to mitigate side-channel attacks is notoriously diffi-
cult. Consequently, its adoption will likely be limited to specialized applications where
communication bandwidth is the dominant constraint.
     Falcon follows the framework for lattice-based hash-and-sign signature schemes
(§8.1) introduced by Gentry, Peikert and Vaikuntanathan (GPV). A prominent feature
of the GPV framework is the need to sample from discrete Gaussian distributions over
lattices; these distributions are detailed in §8.2. After reviewing this framework in §8.3,
we introduce NTRU lattices in §8.4 and describe NTRU key pair generation in §8.5, be-
fore outlining the Falcon scheme itself in §8.6. We briefly explain in §8.7 why Falcon
employs the Fast Fourier Transform.

8.1     Hash-and-sign
8.1.1       RSA signature scheme
The RSA full-domain hash (FDH) signature scheme follows the hash-and-sign paradigm.
Alice’s public key is (N , e) and her private signing key is d = e −1 mod ϕ (N ). To sign a
message M ∈ {0, 1}∗ , she computes h = H (M ), where H : {0, 1}∗ → ZN is a hash
function, and outputs the signature s = hd mod N . To verify a signed message (M, s),
Bob computes h = H (M ) and checks that h = s e mod N .
    The hash value h serves as a random challenge in ZN whose unique preimage under
the RSA permutation is s = hd mod N . Computing this preimage is believed to be infea-
sible without knowledge of d. Thus, d serves as a trapdoor that allows Alice to efficiently

invert the one-way function f : ZN → ZN defined by f (x ) = x e mod N . Such a function
is called a trapdoor one-way function.

8.1.3   SIS-based signature scheme
SIS trapdoor one-way functions naturally yield a hash-and-sign signature scheme anal-
ogous to the RSA full-domain hash signature scheme.
    Alice’s public verification key is the matrix A ∈R Zqn×m , and her private signing key
is a short basis T ∈ Zm×m for the SIS lattice L⊥    A . To sign a message M ∈ {0, 1} , Alice

                                          ∗

    A complete specification requires a method for generating a key pair (A,T ). This
cannot be done by selecting A first and then computing T , as finding short vectors in
arbitrary lattices is hard.
    At first glance, forging a signature appears to require solving an instance of the ap-
proximate closest vector problem (§2.5.3). Indeed, to forge Alice’s signature on a message
M, an adversary can compute u = H (M ) and a target vector t ∈ Zm satisfying At = u
(mod q). The success of the forgery attempt then depends on the adversary’s ability to
find a lattice vector z ∈ L⊥A sufficiently close to t.


8.1.4   A critical security weakness
NTRUSign, the first practical lattice-based signature scheme, employed an SIS-based
trapdoor function over a highly structured lattice called the NTRU lattice (§8.4). This
algebraic structure allowed for compact public keys and signatures. The signing proce-
dure used Babai’s rounding method as described above.
    However, NTRUSign had a critical vulnerability: every signed message (M, s) leaked
geometric information about the secret basis T , specifically revealing that s is confined
to the parallelepiped P 1/2 (T ). Indeed, Nguyen and Regev showed that the secret basis T
could be efficiently reconstructed given a sufficient number of signatures; see Figure 8.1.
For instance, the NTRUSign-251 parameter set, which was designed for 80-bit security,
was completely broken using about 400 signed messages.
    To prevent this leakage, Gentry, Peikert and Vaikuntanathan proposed randomizing
the selection of a preimage s of u = H (M ). The solution bound β is chosen to ensure
that each target u ∈ Zqn is expected to have a large number of preimages, but not render

8.3     GPV signature framework
Gentry, Peikert and Vaikuntanathan (GPV) introduced a framework for secure hash-
and-sign signature schemes. The key ingredient is a preimage-sampleable trapdoor one-
way function. GPV gave a lattice-based construction whose security is based on SIS
hardness. This section describes the lattice-based GPV signature framework, instantiated
concretely by Falcon.

Preliminaries. The size of a basis T = [t 1 , . . . , tm ] is kT k = maxi kti k. The Gram-

Remark 8.14 (sampleable trapdoor one-way functions) The trapdoor function f A satis-
fies two key properties.

    • Domain sampling with uniform outputs. Sample s ∼ D Zm ,s and set u = f A (s) =
      As mod q. The resulting distribution of u is statistically indistinguishable from
      uniform over Zqn .

    • Preimage sampling with trapdoor. Conversely, if u ∈ Zqn is fixed, t ∈ Zm is an
      arbitrary solution to At = u (mod q), and z is sampled from D LA⊥ ,s,t , then the
      distribution of s = t − z is exactly the conditional distribution of D Zm ,s given
      As = u (mod q).

These properties are fundamental to proving that the GPV signature scheme is secure
(Definition A.7) in the random oracle model under SIS hardness. The proof simulates a
signer without T by programming H using the first property: on each new hash query
(M, r ), the simulator samples s directly from D Zm ,s and returns u = f A (s), so that the
§8.4 NTRU lattices                                                                             101


outputs of H remain statistically indistinguishable from uniform. The second property
ensures that this s is distributed as in a real signature, so the simulator answers signing
queries simply by revealing the previously sampled s without ever needing T .

Remark 8.15 (message randomization) The message M is randomized prior to signing
by appending a randomly chosen salt r ∈ {0, 1} ` . To see why randomization is necessary,
suppose Alice signs the same message M twice without a salt. Assuming the same t is
computed both times (as would be the case with any deterministic method for solving
At = u (mod q)), the signatures are s 1 = t − z 1 and s 2 = t − z 2 with z 1 , z 2 ∼ D LA⊥ ,s,t and
s 1 , s 2 except with negligible probability. An adversary learning s 1 and s 2 obtains two
distinct preimages of u = H (M ). Exposing multiple independent samples for the same
target u breaks the GPV security proof, since the reduction can consistently program
the random oracle only if at most one preimage of each target is revealed. Moreover,
s 1 − s 2 = z 2 − z 1 is a short nonzero vector in L⊥

problem for A, giving the adversary information that is presumed infeasible to compute
without knowledge of the secret basis T .

8.5    NTRU key pair generation
This section describes a method for generating an NTRU public key h and the corre-
sponding private key ( f , д, F , G), where h = д/f in Zq [x]/(x n + 1) (which requires f
and x n + 1 to be coprime in Zq [x]) and f , д, F , G ∈ Z[x]/(x n + 1) are short polynomials
satisfying the NTRU equation f G − дF = q modulo x n + 1.
     One might try to select short f and д, verify that gcd( f , x n +1) = 1 in Zq [x], and then
use the extended Euclidean algorithm to compute F 0, G 0 ∈ Z[x] such that f G 0 − дF 0 = 1;
multiplying F 0 and G 0 by q would then solve the NTRU equation. But Z[x] is not a
principal ideal domain, so the extended Euclidean algorithm is unavailable. Moreover,
1 generally does not lie in the ideal generated by f and д so no such F 0, G 0 exist at
all.14 Instead, the algorithm descends to Z, where the extended Euclidean algorithm is
available, by passing from f and д to the integers R f and Rд defined below.

8.6    Falcon outline
Falcon follows the GPV framework for lattice-based hash-and-sign signature schemes.
The key elements of Falcon’s design are: (i) the use of NTRU lattices, which enable
compact public keys and signatures; (ii) a discrete Gaussian sampler utilizing Fast Fourier
Transform (FFT) arithmetic; and (iii) the specification of concrete parameters tailored to
meet specific security levels.
    The intricate implementation details of Falcon, particularly the mechanics of the FFT
sampler, lie beyond our immediate scope. This section provides a high-level outline of
Falcon, aiming to provide a solid foundation for a reader who wishes to embark on a
detailed study of the full specification.

8.7     The Fast Fourier Transform
Much of Falcon’s computational efficiency stems from performing discrete Gaussian
sampling with the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) in floating-point arithmetic; this is also
the root of the side-channel vulnerabilities mentioned in the introduction. This section
overviews why and how Falcon uses the FFT. We omit technical details, which may be
added once FIPS 206 is finalized.

FFT definition. The Number Theoretic Transform (NTT), presented in detail in §13,
provides efficient polynomial multiplication in Rq = Zq [x]/(x n + 1) when n is a power
of two. In contrast, the FFT multiplies polynomials in the real algebra R[x]/(x n + 1) and,
by restriction, in the subrings Q = Q[x]/(x n + 1) and R = Z[x]/(x n + 1).
  15 In this problem, one is given an NTRU public key h and ` targets u , . . . , u ∈ R , and has to find a

Definition 8.27 Let n = 2k and let ζ = e i π /n be a complex primitive 2n-th root of unity.
The Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) is the map DFT : R[x]/(x n + 1) → Cn defined by

                      DFT( f ) = ( f (ζ ), f (ζ 3 ), f (ζ 5 ), . . . , f (ζ 2n−1 )).

    Note that the odd powers of ζ are precisely the complex roots of x n + 1. For no-
tational convenience, we often write fˆ in place of DFT( f ). Addition, subtraction, and
multiplication of polynomials in their DFT representation is componentwise, requiring
O (n) arithmetic operations. Since DFT is invertible, polynomials can be converted be-
tween coefficient and DFT representations.
    The Fast Fourier Transform is an O (n log n) algorithm for computing both DFT and
DFT−1 . Combined with componentwise multiplication, this yields an overall O (n log n)
algorithm for multiplying polynomials f , д ∈ R[x]/(x n + 1):

                             f · д = DFT−1 (DFT( f ) · DFT(д)) .

Since the DFT outputs complex numbers, their real and imaginary parts must be ap-
proximated in practice using floating-point numbers. Falcon utilizes standard IEEE 754
double-precision (64-bit) floating-point numbers for these computations.

FFT sampler. Discrete Gaussian sampling z ∼ D LA⊥ ,σ,t in signature generation uses
Klein’s algorithm, which draws z one coordinate at a time along the Gram-Schmidt or-
thogonalization T̃ of T . Each coordinate is from a one-dimensional discrete Gaussian
with center and width determined by T̃ . The difficulty is that Gram-Schmidt vectors,
and hence per-coordinate centers and widths, are real numbers with no small exact rep-
resentation. Thus T̃ is stored approximately as the Falcon tree, and the sampler uses
IEEE 754 double-precision floating-point.

8.8   Notes and further references
The security of the RSA full-domain hash (FDH) signature scheme in the random oracle
model was analyzed by Bellare and Rogaway [28]. NTRUSign was designed by Hoff-
stein, Howgrave-Graham, Pipher, Silverman and Whyte [109]. Nguyen and Regev [164]
demonstrated attacks on both NTRUSign and an earlier signature scheme by Goldreich,
Goldwasser and Halevi [97]. Their attack reduced the problem of recovering a secret par-
allelepiped from many random points uniformly distributed within it to a multivariate
optimization problem, which they solved using gradient descent. Two countermeasures
were proposed to mask the geometric structure of the secret basis, but Ducas and Nguyen
[74] showed that both were insufficient.
    Micciancio and Regev [154] introduced the smoothing parameter. Theorems 8.7,
8.10 and 8.11, correspond to footnote 12, Lemma 4.1, and Lemma 4.4 of their paper, re-
spectively. Theorem 8.12 is due to Gentry, Peikert and Vaikuntanathan [92, 93]. Algo-
rithms for sampling from discrete Gaussian distributions on lattices were surveyed by
Dwarakanath and Galbraith [77].
§8.8 Notes and further references                                                       116


    The notion of a sampleable trapdoor one-way function was formulated by Gentry,
Peikert and Vaikuntanathan (GPV) [92, 93], who showed how to construct these prim-
itives from lattices for use in hash-and-sign signature schemes and identity-based en-
cryption schemes, and proved the claims in Remark 8.14. The GPV signature scheme
uses Ajtai’s algorithm [5] for selecting (A,T ) and Klein’s algorithm [123] for sampling
from discrete Gaussians. Alwen and Peikert [15] improved Ajtai’s algorithm, reducing
the size of the Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization T̃ of the trapdoor basis T is reduced from
            √
m2.5 to O ( m).
    GPV gave a tight proof (cf. Remark 8.14) that their signature scheme is strongly se-
cure in the random oracle model (ROM), where the hash function H is modelled as a
uniformly random oracle accessible to all parties. Boneh, Dagdelen and Fischlin [34]
subsequently proved its security in the quantum random oracle model (QROM), where
the adversary may query H in quantum superposition.
    Micciancio and Peikert [153] introduced lattice-based trapdoor functions that are
conceptually simpler and more efficient than the original GPV construction. Unlike GPV,
which samples preimages via a randomized nearest-plane procedure, the Micciancio-
Peikert method employs a public “gadget” m ×n matrix G (with m > n) for which preim-
ages of the SIS function fG T (x ) = GT x (mod q) can be efficiently sampled from a discrete
Gaussian distribution, and the LWE function дG (s, e) = Gs +e (mod q) can be efficiently
inverted. The secret trapdoor is a short matrix R that relates a random-looking public
matrix A to the structured gadget matrix G, enabling efficient preimage sampling or in-
version while ensuring that the corresponding SIS problem for AT and the LWE problem
for A remain computationally hard. Two prominent applications are the fully homomor-
phic encryption scheme of Gentry, Sahai and Waters [94] and the predicate encryption
scheme of Gorbunov, Vaikuntanathan and Wee [100].
    The NTRU public-key encryption scheme and the notion of an NTRU lattice were
proposed in 1996 by Hoffstein, Pipher and Silverman [110]. In the original NTRU design,
the secret polynomials f and д are chosen from the ring Zq [x]/(x n − 1) with coefficients
in {−1, 0, 1}. Stehlé and Steinfeld [195] proposed instead using the power-of-two cy-
clotomic ring Rq = Zq [x]/(x n + 1), where the coefficients of f , д ∈ Z[x]/(x n + 1) are
sampled from a discrete Gaussian distribution of width poly(n) ·q 1/2+ε . They proved that
the resulting public key h = д/f ∈ Rq is statistically indistinguishable from the uniform
distribution over Rq . Algorithm 8.23 for NTRU key pair generation is derived from the
NTRUSign paper by Hoffstein et al. [109].
    Ducas, Lyubashevsky and Prest [73] realized the GPV signature scheme (and identity-
based encryption scheme) using NTRU lattices, demonstrating for the first time that the
GPV signature framework could be made practically efficient with respect to computa-
tional speed, public-key size, and signature size.
    Ducas and Prest [75] showed how the Cooley-Tukey fast Fourier Transform (FFT)
[59] could be adapted to substantially accelerate Klein’s algorithm [123] for discrete
Gaussian sampling. Klein’s algorithm is a randomized variant of Babai’s nearest plane
algorithm [19] for finding a lattice vector close to a given target. The Ducas-Prest al-
gorithm precomputes the Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization of the trapdoor lattice basis

in the form of a tree. Using this tree, discrete Gaussian sampling can be performed in
time O (n log n). A detailed exposition of the FFT-based Gaussian sampling method can
be found in Prest’s Ph.D. thesis [182].
    Falcon was designed by Fouque et al. [83], building on the GPV framework. In Fal-
con, NTRU key pair generation uses the efficient algorithm of Pornin and Prest [180],
                                                    `
which exploits the tower of subfields of Q[x]/(x 2 + 1) as noted in Remark 8.25. This
method reduces both computation time and RAM usage by two orders of magnitude
compared to prior algebraic approaches. Falcon also employs the aforementioned Ducas-
Prest FFT-based discrete Gaussian sampling method; the FFT-tree representation of the
Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization of the trapdoor lattice basis is called the Falcon tree. In
2024, Fouque, Gajland, de Groote, Janneck and Kiltz [81, 82] gave the first security proof
of Falcon. Their proof is in the random oracle model and assumes the hardness of the
multi-target inhomogeneous SIS problem over NTRU lattices.
    Hardware accelerators for Falcon have been designed by Beckwith, Nguyen and Gaj
[27] as well as Ouyang et al. [176]. Meanwhile, high-throughput GPU implementations
have been developed by Lee et al. [133] and Li et al. [138]. Notably, the latter achieved
signing throughputs of 172,000 and 90,000 signatures per second for Falcon-512 and
Falcon-1024, respectively, on an NVIDIA A100 (80GB PCIe) GPU.
    Several authors have highlighted vulnerabilities of the discrete Gaussian samplers
and floating-point arithmetic to side-channel attacks. Fouque, Kirchner, Tibouchi, Wal-
let and Yu [84] demonstrated timing attacks on Falcon; Guerreau, Martinelli, Ricosset
and Rossi [102] alongside Zhang, Lin, Yu and Wang [205] introduced power analysis at-
tacks; and Haidar, Payet and Tibouchi [104] investigated fault-injection attacks. These
attacks all target discrete Gaussian sampling and recover the secret key. For instance, the
power-analysis attack by Zhang et al. recovers a Falcon-512 secret key in roughly half
an hour using power traces from approximately 45,000 signatures. Furthermore, Lin,
Tibouchi, Yu and Zhang [139] observed that the sampler is highly sensitive to floating-
point errors when executed twice with identical inputs; such a scenario might occur if a
signer improperly reuses a salt on the same message.

     FrodoKEM is a quantum-safe key encapsulation mechanism (KEM) standardized by
ISO in 2026. Like Kyber-KEM, FrodoKEM is based on the Lindner-Peikert encryption
scheme (§4.2). However, its parameter choices are more conservative. In particular,
FrodoKEM relies on the hardness of standard LWE in unstructured lattices, in contrast
to Kyber-KEM, which relies on the hardness of the module-LWE problem over algebraic
lattices. Additionally, FrodoKEM samples its errors from a discrete approximation to
a rounded Gaussian rather than from a centered binomial distribution, thereby match-
ing more closely the Gaussian noise of Regev’s worst-case to average-case reduction for
LWE (§4.4.4).16
     We begin in §9.1 with the error distribution used by FrodoKEM. We then introduce
the underlying public-key encryption scheme, FrodoPKE, in §9.2. Finally, §9.3 presents
the full FrodoKEM construction, derived via a suitably modified Fujisaki-Okamoto trans-
formation.

9.2.1   FrodoPKE
FrodoPKE is presented in Algorithm 9.7. It is structurally similar to the Kyber public-
key encryption scheme (Algorithm 6.1), but is based on standard LWE, working with
matrices whose entries are in Zq rather than in a polynomial ring. The modulus q is a
power of two, namely q = 215 for the FrodoKEM-640 parameter set and q = 216 for the
FrodoKEM-976 and FrodoKEM-1344 parameter sets. This choice simplifies both modular
reduction and the encoding of messages. See Table 9.3 for the three FrodoKEM parameter
sets.
    The pseudorandom bit generator ExpandA, instantiated using either SHAKE128 or
AES128, produces a matrix in Zqn×n from a 128-bit seed. The pseudorandom bit gener-
ator ExpandSE, instantiated using SHAKE128 for the FrodoKEM-640 parameter set and
using SHAKE256 for the FrodoKEM-976 and FrodoKEM-1344 parameter sets, produces
matrices S, E ∈ Λn×n from a 2`-bit seed where Λ = {−c, −c + 1, . . . , c − 1, c}; each of the
entries of these matrices is sampled independently from the distribution χ = χs,c . The
pseudorandom bit generator ExpandRE likewise produces matrices R, E 1 ∈ Λn×n and
E 2 ∈ Λn×n from a 2`-bit seed, with entries again sampled independently from χ . The

9.2.3    Security
The security of FrodoPKE rests on ss-D-MatrixLWE, which differs from the short-secret
decisional LWE problem of Definition 4.10 in three respects:

   (i) the modulus q is a power of two rather than a prime;
  (ii) the secret and error terms are sampled from a discrete approximation to a rounded
       Gaussian distribution χ on (a subset of) Zq rather than from the uniform distribu-
       tion on a short interval centered at 0; and
 (iii) the same matrix A is shared across n instances, one for each column of the secret
       matrix.

least as hard as ss-DLWE. As a warm-up, we first prove the corresponding statement for
the search problems, that MatrixLWE is at least as hard as LWE.

9.3   FrodoKEM
As in the construction of Kyber-KEM, FrodoKEM is derived by applying a variant of the
Fujisaki-Okamoto transform to FrodoPKE, though the variant here additionally incor-
porates a salt. This transformation converts a public-key encryption scheme that is only
indistinguishable under chosen-plaintext attack (Definition A.2) into a KEM attaining a
stronger notion of security, namely indistinguishability under chosen-ciphertext attack
(Definition A.5). The guarantee holds in the (quantum) random oracle model.
    FrodoKEM is shown in Algorithm 9.16. The pseudorandom bit generators ExpandA,
ExpandSE and ExpandRE are the ones used in FrodoPKE. The variable-output length
hash function H , which maps input x ∈ {0, 1}∗ and a length parameter d ≥ 1 to an
output H (x, d ) ∈ {0, 1}d , is instantiated using either SHAKE128 (for FrodoKEM-640) or
SHAKE256 (for FrodoKEM-976 and FrodoKEM-1344).
    FrodoPKE is employed to encrypt a randomly chosen bit string m of length `. Dur-
ing encapsulation, derandomization is applied as in Kyber-KEM, whereby the hashed
encapsulation key ekh, the message m and a freshly chosen salt are hashed to produce
a random seed seedRE and a secret k. The random matrices R, E 1 and E 2 required for
FrodoPKE are derived from seedRE , and the shared secret key K is derived by hashing
the ciphertext and the secret k. Unlike Kyber-KEM, however, encapsulation is not deter-
ministic in m and EK alone, since a fresh salt is chosen each time. The salt is transmitted
in the clear as part of the ciphertext C = (U , V , salt), so that decapsulation can reproduce
seedRE and k. The transform does not require determinism as such; it requires only that
Bob be able to recompute the randomness used during encryption.
    The salt was incorporated in response to an analysis showing that the multi-ciphertext
security of lattice-based encryption schemes degrades as the number of ciphertexts un-
der a single public key grows; see Exercise 9.7.
    In decapsulation, the recipient decrypts the FrodoPKE ciphertext (U , V ) to recover
m , then hashes ekh, m 0 and the salt received in C to obtain seedRE
