encrypts m using seedRE and compares the resulting (U , V ) with the received (U , V ).

9.4     Notes and further references
Frodo was first proposed as an LWE-based key agreement protocol by Bos et al. [40] in
2016. The derived KEM, FrodoKEM, was submitted to the NIST Post-Quantum Cryptog-
raphy project by Alkim et al. [12]. It advanced to Round 3 as an alternate candidate but
was not selected for standardization, with NIST citing its bandwidth and performance
costs relative to the structured-lattice finalists. Nevertheless, several agencies have en-
dorsed FrodoKEM as a conservative alternative to structured-lattice schemes, including
Germany’s BSI, France’s ANSSI, the Netherlands’ NLNCSA, and the European Union
Agency for Cybersecurity. In June 2026, ISO standardized FrodoKEM, together with
ML-KEM and Classic McEliece, as part of ISO/IEC 18033-2 [117].
    In 2023 the FrodoKEM designers added a salt to the Fujisaki-Okamoto transform
[86, 111] in response to a multi-ciphertext security degradation observed by Bernstein
[29]. At the same time they specified an ephemeral variant, eFrodoKEM, which omits the
salt and shortens seedS E and seedRE to ` bits. Because it lacks these countermeasures,
eFrodoKEM is intended only for settings in which a single encapsulation key is used
§9.5 Exercises                                                                                         137


to produce a small number of ciphertexts (e.g., fewer than 28 ). Glabush et al. [96] give a
comprehensive description and analysis of FrodoKEM and eFrodoKEM, including details
of the ExpandA, ExpandSE and ExpandRE pseudorandom bit generators.
    The distribution χs,c is only an approximation to the rounded Gaussian Ψs , whereas
the worst-case to average-case reductions underlying the security of LWE are stated for
the exact distribution. Bounding the resulting security loss by the statistical distance
between the two would require an approximation accurate to within 2−λ , where λ is
the security level, and hence a sampler using far more than 16 bits of precision. The
FrodoKEM designers instead bound the loss using the Rényi divergence, following Lan-
glois, Stehlé and Steinfeld [131]; see also Bai et al. [21] for a systematic treatment. This
tolerates a much coarser approximation, at the cost of only a small loss in the concrete
security estimate.

    The LLL algorithm, also known as L3 , is a polynomial-time algorithm that finds a
relatively short and nearly orthogonal basis of a lattice. It was discovered in 1982 by
Arjen Lenstra, Hendrik Lenstra, and László Lovász. Its first major application was a
polynomial-time algorithm for factoring polynomials with rational coefficients. Since
then, LLL has become a fundamental tool in computational number theory and cryptog-
raphy. Most notably, it is used to solve the Shortest Vector Problem (SVP) and its variant
approx-SVP which, as we saw in §3 and §4, plays a central role in assessing the security
of lattice-based cryptosystems.
    The remainder of this section is organized as follows. In §10.1, we review the Gram-
Schmidt orthogonalization process, a key ingredient of the LLL algorithm. Gauss’s al-
gorithm for computing a shortest basis of a two-dimensional integer lattice is presented
in §10.2. The LLL algorithm itself is described and analyzed in §10.3, followed by an
overview of several improvements in §10.4.

original one.

v − cu, and then swap u and the new v to maintain the ordering ku k ≤ kv k. This
procedure terminates once c = 0, which occurs exactly when |µ | ≤ 12 .

10.3     The LLL algorithm
Let L be an n-dimensional integer lattice. As with Gauss’s reduction in two dimensions,
it is not difficult to find a lattice basis B = [b1 , . . . , bn ] so that the Gram-Schmidt coeffi-
cients µ i j are small, specifically |µ i j | ≤ 12 for 1 ≤ j < i ≤ n. This condition, known as
size reduction, ensures that the basis vectors are reasonably close to being orthogonal.
However, it does not guarantee that the basis vectors themselves are short.
     Consider a randomly chosen lattice basis B. One expects that the Gram-Schmidt
vectors b1∗ , . . . , bn∗ rapidly decrease in length. This is because each vector bi∗ is obtained
by projecting bi onto the orthogonal complement of the subspace spanned by the ear-
lier basis vectors b1 , . . . , bi−1 . As i increases, this orthogonal complement has smaller
dimension, and consequently the projection of bi typically tends to be shorter.
     A key invariant of lattices comes into play here. Although the individual Gram-
Schmidt vectors depend on the chosen lattice basis, the product of their lengths does
not—it is equal to the volume of the lattice (see Theorem 10.8). The central idea behind
the LLL algorithm is to exploit this fact by reshaping the lattice basis so that the lengths
of the Gram-Schmidt vectors are distributed more evenly, rather than dropping off too
quickly.
     The mechanism that makes this possible is a sequence of local operations: size reduc-
tion and swaps of adjacent basis vectors. The swaps are designed to slow down the rate
at which the Gram-Schmidt lengths decrease, thereby forcing earlier vectors to become
relatively short. In particular, the first vector b1∗ is expected to be relatively short, and
thus so will the first lattice basis vector b1 (since b1 = b1∗ ). More precisely, we will prove
that the first vector in the lattice basis produced by the LLL algorithm is guaranteed to
have length no more than 2 (n−1)/2 times the length of a shortest nonzero lattice vector.

10.3.3       Algorithm description
The LLL lattice basis reduction algorithm (Algorithm 10.20) begins by size reducing the
input basis. It then swaps two adjacent basis vectors b j−1 and b j for which the Lovász

By Theorem 10.26, the total number of iterations executed by the LLL algorithm is poly-

10.3.6   A dimension-15 example
We conclude this section with a more substantial illustration of the LLL algorithm.

Example 10.33 (LLL algorithm) We start with a randomly-chosen basis for a full-rank
integer lattice L in fifteen dimensions. Each coordinate of the basis vectors was sampled
uniformly at random from the interval [−2, 2]. This initial basis is displayed in Fig-
ure 10.6. By construction, the basis vectors are quite short, with lengths ranging from

in Figure 10.7.

10.4.3    Using floating point arithmetic
Recall that the running time of LLL is O (n6 log3 X ) bit operations, where n is the lattice
dimension and X denotes the maximum length of the input basis vectors. During its
execution, the algorithm performs arithmetic operations on integers whose bitlengths
are on the order of O (n log X ). In practical settings, the value of X can be quite large.
For instance, in applications to the analysis of RSA implementations, X may be 2048
bits or more. For such large values of X , the O (log3 X ) dependence in the running time
becomes a major computational bottleneck. As a result, the original LLL algorithm is
typically practical only for lattices of relatively small dimensions.
    When working with higher-dimensional lattices, it is therefore common to replace
the exact integer arithmetic with floating point arithmetic in the computation of the
Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization B ∗ and coefficients µ i j . While this modification sub-
stantially improves efficiency, it also introduces the possibility of rounding errors which,
in some cases, may prevent the algorithm from terminating or may result in a basis that
is not LLL-reduced.
    To address these difficulties, Nguyen and Stehlé proposed a floating-point version
of LLL, which they called L2 . In their algorithm, the Gram-Schmidt computations are
performed using floating-point arithmetic with a precision of approximately 1.58n bits.
Notably, this precision is independent of the length X of the input basis vectors. The
running time of L2 has the important feature that it depends only on log2 X , rather than
log3 X as in the original LLL algorithm.

10.5    Notes and further references
Gauss described his lattice basis reduction algorithm in 1801.
The algorithm was, in fact, first discovered by Lagrange in 1773,
but this was not well known until quite recently, and so the algo-
rithm is commonly called Gauss’s algorithm. The polynomial-
time complexity of Gauss’s algorithm was established by La-
garias [128]. Vallée [199] derived the best possible upper bound
on the number of iterations, and explored the connection be-
tween Gauss’s algorithm and Euclid’s algorithm for computing
the greatest common divisor of two integers. Nguyen and Stehlé
[168] showed that the running time of Gauss’s algorithm can be improved to O (log2 X )
bit operations, where X is the length of the longer of the two input basis vectors.
    The LLL algorithm was introduced by Lenstra, Lenstra and Lovász [135] in their
landmark 1982 paper, which also derived its O (n6 log3 X ) bit complexity stated in Theo-
rem 10.30, and presented the first polynomial-time algorithm for factoring polynomials
over the rational numbers. The book The LLL Algorithm: Survey and Applications, edited
by Nguyen and Vallée [171], contains a collection of articles covering algorithmic aspects
of lattice reduction, applications to algorithmic number theory, integer programming,
and cryptography, as well as the complexity of lattice problems. Chapter 1 provides an
interesting historical account of the development of the LLL algorithm.
    Stehlé [194] studied practical and theoretical aspects of floating-point variants of
LLL. The L2 variant of LLL was introduced by Nguyen and Stehlé [167]. Nguyen and
Stehlé [166] reported extensive experimental results on the average-case behaviour of L2 ,
aiming to explain the significant gap between its practical performance and the proven
worst-case bounds. Specifically, they studied the algorithm’s behaviour on rank-d in-
teger lattices L ⊆ Rn with n = Θ(d ), whose bases are randomly generated with vector
lengths bounded by X , where d = O (log X ). Their experiments indicate that the average-
case estimate of the Hermite factor, defined as kb1 k/ vol(L) 1/d for the first vector b1 of the
output basis, is approximately 1.02d . This represents a substantial improvement over the
worst-case bound of (4/3)d /4 ≈ 1.075d for δ ≈ 1; see equation (90). Most LLL-reduced
bases do attain this worst-case upper bound, as shown by Kim and Venkatesh [121]. Fur-
§10.6 Exercises                                                                                        169


thermore, while the worst-case analysis requires about 1.58d bits of numerical precision,
the average-case analysis suggests that about 0.25d bits suffice in practice. These exper-
imental findings were further corroborated by Gama and Nguyen [88]. A recent LLL
implementation incorporating several theoretical improvements is described by Ducas,
Pulles and Stevens [76].

    Block Korkine-Zolotarev (BKZ) is a blockwise generalization of the LLL algorithm,
introduced by Schnorr and Euchner in 1994. Rather than operating on the entire lattice
at once, BKZ repeatedly solves SVP instances in certain low-dimensional lattices called
blocks. These blocks have dimension β, called the blocksize, where β is typically much
smaller than the full lattice dimension n. Each SVP instance is solved by an SVP oracle,
usually implemented via either enumeration or sieving, both of which have exponential
running times; enumeration is described in §11.4, and sieving in §11.5. There is a fun-
damental tradeoff in the choice of the blocksize: larger values of β typically produce
higher-quality reduced bases, but at the cost of a substantial increase in running time.
When β = 2, the BKZ algorithm coincides with the original LLL algorithm (i.e., with
parameter δ = 1).
    Although precise cost estimates for BKZ remain difficult to obtain, extensive experi-
mental evidence shows that BKZ significantly outperforms LLL in practice. In particular,
BKZ has been used to solve the hardest SVP challenges, and BKZ running-time estimates
play a central role in assessing the hardness of SVP and approx-SVP instances that arise
in the security analysis of Kyber and Dilithium. These estimates, in turn, underpin the
selection and justification of the standardized parameter sets for these schemes.

11.2     Algorithm description
No efficient algorithm for computing a β-BKZ-reduced basis of a lattice L ⊆ Rn is known.
This is not surprising since, as noted above, the first vector of an n-BKZ-reduced basis
solves SVP in L, which is NP-hard. Moreover, as shown in Theorem 11.3, a 2-BKZ-
reduced basis is a 1-LLL-reduced basis, and no polynomial-time algorithm is known for
finding the latter.
    The BKZ algorithm (Algorithm 11.6) begins with an LLL-reduced basis B = [b1 , . . . , bn ]
and repeatedly performs tours until a β-BKZ-reduced basis is obtained. A tour consists
of a sequence of n − 1 block operations. The first n − β + 1 block operations act on the
length-β blocks B[i, i + β − 1] for 1 ≤ i ≤ n − β + 1. The remaining β − 2 block operations
act on the smaller blocks B[i, n] for n − β + 2 ≤ i ≤ n − 1, whose lengths decrease from
β − 1 down to 2.
    Like the LLL swap operation, the BKZ block operation (Algorithm 11.7) is a lo-
cal modification of a lattice basis, designed to prevent the Gram-Schmidt vectors from

11.3     Complexity analysis
The BKZ algorithm is guaranteed to terminate after at most O (β n ) tours. This fact im-
plies that, for any lattice, a β-BKZ-reduced basis always exists. However, it remains an
open question whether the number of tours can be bounded by a polynomial in the lat-
tice dimension n. In practical implementations, BKZ is terminated after successive tours
no longer produce a significant improvement in the quality of the basis. The complexity
analysis presented here assumes such early-abort strategies are employed.

11.4    Enumeration
Enumeration is a method for solving SVP, i.e., finding a shortest nonzero vector in a
lattice L(B) ⊆ Zn . Although its running time is fully exponential in the lattice dimension
n, enumeration has the advantage of requiring very little memory.
      The algorithm begins with an upper bound D on the first successive minimum λ 1 (L).
It then systematically enumerates integer vectors x ∈ Zn satisfying 0 < kx k ≤ D, and
outputs a lattice vector of shortest length found during the search. By first applying
the LLL algorithm, we may assume without loss of generality that the lattice basis B =
[b1 , . . . , bn ] is LLL-reduced. Minkowski’s Theorem provides a natural upper bound for
λ 1 (L):                                         √
                                   D = min(kb1 k, n vol(L) 1/n ).                     (102)

Naive enumeration. A naive approach to finding a shortest nonzero lattice vector
involves enumerating all candidate vectors v = (v 1 , . . . , vn ) ∈ [−D, D]n one coordinate
at a time and testing each for membership in L. This can be done systematically using a
depth-first search tree of height n. The root, at level 0, is denoted by R. For each 1 ≤ i ≤ n,
nodes at level i are labelled by the admissible integer values of vi . Consequently, each
internal node has 2D + 1 children, and the leaves correspond precisely to the vectors in
[−D, D]n . A node z at level i represents the partial vector (v 1 , . . . , vi ), whose coordinates
are the labels of nodes along the unique path from R to z. During the depth-first traversal,
the search tree can be pruned by maintaining the length of the current partial vector. If
this partial length exceeds either the bound D or the length of the shortest nonzero lattice
vector found so far, the corresponding branch is discarded and the algorithm backtracks,
since no extension of the current partial vector can yield a shorter lattice vector. In the

11.5    Sieving
Sieving is a probabilistic method for solving SVP in an integer lattice L ⊆ Zn . Whereas
sieving algorithms are conceptually quite simple, their analysis can be very complicated.
In this section, we will outline the Nguyen-Vidick sieving algorithm and give a simplified
heuristic analysis.

Overview. The algorithm begins with a set S 0 of N 0 ≈ n3 (4/3) n/2 randomly sampled
lattice vectors each of length approximately R 0 , for some R 0 ≤ 2O (n) λ 1 (L). Let γ < 1 be a
shrinking factor; for the sake of concreteness, we will take γ = 1 − n1 . For k = 1, 2, 3, . . .,
the algorithm iteratively applies a sieving step to Sk −1 to produce a set Sk of lattice vectors
each of which has length approximately Rk = γ k R 0 ; see Figure 11.1. Notably, the sets do
not significantly decrease in size, so Sk has size Nk ≈ N 0 . However, once Rk ≈ λ 1 (L), the
sets Sk rapidly decrease in size and inevitably collapse, namely S ` = ∅. In that event, the
shortest vector in S `−1 is expected to have length close to λ 1 (L).

The Nguyen-Vidick sieving algorithm. A simplified version of the sieving method
is given in Algorithm 11.15. The algorithm begins by applying LLL to the input basis B
to obtain an LLL-reduced basis. This ensures that the basis vectors are relatively short,
which in turn allows us to sample23 lattice vectors of length less than 2n λ 1 (L). The initial
radius R 0 is then computed as the maximum length of the vectors in S 0 .
    The main loop iteratively applies a sieving step to the current set Sk and produces a
new set Sk +1 of lattice vectors of length approximately γ Rk . Each sieving step maintains
a set C of “centers”, which are vectors in Sk possessing the property that the distance
between any two centers is greater than γ Rk . The sieving step processes every vector
v ∈ Sk . If v has length at most γ Rk , it is inserted in Sk +1 . Otherwise, either v − c is
inserted in Sk+1 if v ∈ Bn (c, γ Rk ) for some c ∈ C, or else v is identified as a center. After
processing all v ∈ Sk , the radius Rk +1 is computed as the maximum length of the vectors
in Sk+1 .
    The sieving continues until the set Sk is empty, meaning no further reductions are
possible. As we will discuss in the analysis below, this occurs once Rk ≈ λ 1 (L). The
algorithm then returns the shortest vector in the final nonempty set, which is expected
to have length close to λ 1 (L).

Analysis. We now give a heuristic analysis of the sieving algorithm. The analysis rests
on the following key heuristic assumption.

Heuristic assumption 1 For each k ≥ 0, the unit vectors {v/kv k : v ∈ Sk } are inde-
pendently and uniformly distributed on the unit sphere S.
    While this assumption is not provably true, it is supported by experiment and is
standard in the lattice sieving literature. It allows us to treat the normalized vectors in
each set Sk as random points on the unit sphere.
    We first justify that the size N 0 of the initial set S 0 is sufficient to sustain the sieve,
meaning that Nk ≈ N 0 , where Nk = |Sk |. We’ll assume that every vector in Sk has
size approximately Rk ≈ γ k R 0 . Since the sieve is scale-invariant, we may normalize all
vectors in Sk to lie on the unit sphere S without loss of generality. Fix a vector c ∈ Sk .
Since γ ≈ 1, we can use Lemma 11.14 to conclude that the probability a vector v ∈ S
satisfies kv − c k ≤ γ is approximately √1n (3/4) n/2 . In other words, each vector c ∈ Sk
“covers” a √1n (3/4) n/2 fraction of the sphere, in the sense that any unit vector v falling
within this fraction will yield a shorter vector v −c. For the sieve to be sustainable, every
vector on the sphere must be covered by at least one vector in Sk . Assuming the covered
regions have negligible overlap, a set of size N covers a √Nn (3/4) n/2 fraction of the sphere.

11.8    Notes and further references
Yasuda [203] surveys algorithms for solving SVP, including LLL, BKZ, sieving, and enu-
meration. A more recent survey that covers the latest advances in LLL, BKZ, enumera-
tion, and sieving is provided by Shen and Li [192].
      The notion of a β-BKZ-reduced basis was introduced by Schnorr [187]. The upper
bound in Theorem 11.5 on the length of the first vector in a β-BKZ-reduced        p basis B =
[b1 , . . . , bn ] was proved by Schnorr [188], who also showed that kbi k ≤ (i + 3)/4 ·
  (n−1)/(β −1)
γβ                λi (L) for 2 ≤ i ≤ n. The BKZ algorithm is due to Schnorr and Euchner
[190]. The modified-LLL algorithm, which produces an LLL-reduced basis when the
input is a linearly dependent spanning set rather than a true basis, was first described
by Pohst [178]; see also Section 2.6.4 of Cohen [56]. Hanrot, Pujol and Stehlé [105]
proved that a slightly modified version of the BKZ algorithm terminates after O (β n )
tours, which implies the existence of β-BKZ-reduced bases. In 2011, Chen and Nguyen
[53] introduced BKZ 2.0, a refined version of BKZ designed with early abort. See also the
article by Albrecht, Player and Scott [10], which performs a detailed analysis of BKZ 2.0
and gives concrete estimates for various families of LWE instances. The first rigorous
analysis of BKZ was given by Li and Nguyen [137]. Running-time estimates for BKZ
were used by Bos et al. [41] to assess the security of Kyber, and by Ducas et al. [72] to
assess the security of Dilithium.
      The basic enumeration algorithm was described by Kannan [118]. The algorithm
can be optimized to have running time O (2n log n ). Although enumeration algorithms
are asymptotically slower than sieving, they require only modest amounts of memory.
Schnorr and Euchner [190] introduced a method for pruning the search tree, and later
an improved pruning method was proposed by Gama, Nguyen and Regev [89].
      Sieving methods are the fastest algorithms known for solving SVP exactly. Siev-
ing was originally proposed by Ajtai, Kumar and Sivakumar [7], who also showed that
approx-SVP with approximation factor γ > 2 (n log log n)/ log n is solvable in polynomial
time. The sieving algorithm presented in §11.5, together with Theorem 11.10, is due to
Nguyen and Vidick [172]. In Nguyen and Vidick’s sieving algorithm, the vectors in the
original list S 0 are selected according to a Gaussian distribution using Klein’s algorithm
[123]. Nguyen and Vidick give a more careful analysis than the one given in §11.5, and
also provide experimental evidence for the validity of Heuristic Assumption 1. Theo-
rem 11.11 appears in Cai, Fan and Jiang [45].
      Micciancio and Voulgaris [155] proposed GaussSieve, which performs well in prac-
tice. The fastest classical sieving algorithm, due to Becker, Ducas, Gama and Laarhoven
[26], uses locality sensitive hashing to speed up the search for nearby lattice vectors, and
runs in time 20.292n+o (n) . The fastest quantum variant, described by Bonnetain, Chail-
loux, Schrottenloher and Shen [38], runs in time 20.256n+o (n) . While these running times
are heuristic, the fastest known classical SVP solvers with rigorously proven running
times are the 20.73134n+o (n) -time randomized algorithm of Gao, Feng and Hu [91] which
returns a shortest nonzero lattice vector with probability 1−2−Ω(n log n) , the 20.63269n+o (n) -
time algorithm of Pouly and Shen [181] which succeeds for most random lattices, and
§11.9 Exercises                                                                      196


the 20.6039n+o (n) -time randomized algorithm of Hhan [108]. Aggarwal and Stephens-
Davidowitz [1] described a conceptually simple sieving algorithm that provably runs in
time 2n+o (n) and space 2n+o (n) .
    A notable drawback of sieving-based methods is that they require both exponential
time and exponential space. Zhao, Ding and Yang [207] report on their solution in 2024
of a dimension-183 SVP challenge using sieving; their computation required 30 days on a
112-core server with 0.87 Terabytes of RAM. More recently, Zhao and Ding [206] report
on their solution of a dimension-200 SVP challenge using sieving; their computation
required 30 days on a server with eight RTX 4090 GPUs, 1 Terabyte of RAM, and 30
Terabytes of disk space.
    The strategy of using the primal attack together with BKZ reduction to evaluate the
concrete security of Kyber was first proposed by Alkim, Ducas, Pöppelman and Schwabe
[13] in their work introducing the Ring-LWE-based key agreement protocol NewHope.
This paper also introduced the notion of core-SVP hardness. The primal attack strat-
egy was developed further by Bos et al. [41] in the CRYSTALS-Kyber submission to the
NIST post-quantum standardization process. A method for recovering the target vector
x from the projected vector x 0 was described and analyzed by Albrecht, Göpfert, Virdia
and Wunderer [9]. They also gave experimental evidence supporting the accuracy of
the security estimates, showing that the practical behaviour of the primal attack closely
matches the theoretical predictions.
    The Geometric Series Assumption (111) was introduced by Schnorr [189]. The asymp-
totic limit (116) for the root Hermite factor of β-BKZ-reduced bases of random lattices is
due to Chen [52]. An efficient algorithm for simulating the lengths of the Gram-Schmidt
basis vectors after each tour in the BKZ algorithm was presented by Chen and Nguyen
[53].
    Module-BKZ is a generalization of BKZ to module lattices, such as those arising in
the study of MLWE. It was introduced by Lee, Pellet-Mary, Stehlé and Wallet [132], and
by Mukherjee and Stephens-Davidowitz [156]. The average-case behaviour of module-
BKZ was later analyzed by Ducas, Engelberts and de Perthuis [71] and by de Perthuis
and Trenkić [68]. These works did not find any improvement in primal attacks on MLWE
compared to the corresponding attacks on LWE. More recently, Hou, Jiang and Ogilvie
[112] presented an enhanced primal hybrid attack, as well as an improvement to the
dual hybrid attack of Carrier, Meyer-Hilfiger, Shen and Tillich [46]. They showed that
these attacks perform slightly better against MLWE than against unstructured LWE.
Based on this analysis, they estimate that the core-SVP hardness of standardized Kyber
is approximately 1 bit lower than previously believed.

     The general methodology for applying the LLL algorithm proceeds as follows. One
first constructs a lattice L in which the (unknown) solution to the problem at hand is
encoded by a nonzero lattice vector v that is significantly shorter than the Gaussian
heuristic (8) predicts for a shortest nonzero lattice vector. The LLL algorithm is then
applied to compute a reduced basis B of L. Although LLL does not guarantee recovery of
a shortest nonzero lattice vector, in practice its performance is often substantially better
than suggested by the worst-case bounds, and in many practical instances the target
vector v appears among the vectors of the reduced basis. One then inspects the basis
B to determine whether v has been recovered; if so, the original problem can be solved
efficiently.
     This section illustrates this methodology through six applications of the LLL algo-
rithm. The first application is the primal attack on short-secret LWE that was presented
in §11.6. The second application is the dual attack on SIS2 discussed previously in §3.3.
The third application, discussed in §12.3, concerns the discovery of integer relations
among real numbers. This problem is mainly of theoretical interest and may be skipped
by readers whose primary focus is cryptographic applications. The fourth application,
simultaneous Diophantine approximation, presented in §12.4, arises naturally in numer-
ous cryptanalytic settings. The fifth application, described in §12.5, is a concrete side-
channel attack on the ECDSA signature scheme. Lastly, §12.6 introduces a technique
based on LLL for finding small roots of a univariate polynomial modulo a composite
integer with unknown factorization; this technique has found numerous applications
to problems related to RSA and integer factorization. Some other LLL applications are
explored in the Exercises including solving approximate CVP (Exercises 12.5 and 12.6),
solving the subset sum problem (Exercise 12.13), and writing a prime as a sum of four
squares (Exercise 12.14).

12.3    Finding integer relations
Let β = (β 1 , β 2 , . . . , βn ) be a vector of real numbers. An integer relation for β is a linear
combination
                                        c 1 β 1 + c 2 β 2 + · · · + c n βn = 0,                (122)
where c 1 , c 2 , . . . , c n are integers. An integer relation algorithm attempts to find such a
nonzero vector c = (c 1 , c 2 , . . . , c n ), preferably with small coordinates, or determines that
no nontrivial relation exists.

                                        c 1α 1 + c 2α 2 + · · · + c n α n = 0,

12.5        Side-channel attack on ECDSA
The LLL lattice basis reduction algorithm, together with refinements such as BKZ, has
played a central role in the cryptanalysis of many public-key cryptosystems. One of
the earliest and most striking applications of LLL was the successful cryptanalysis of
knapsack-based public-key encryption schemes. These schemes, based on the subset
sum problem, were among the very first public-key proposals of the 1970s. Since then,
LLL-based techniques have also been applied to RSA, DSA, and ECDSA, especially in
settings where partial information about secret key material is exposed. Such leakage can
result from flawed implementations, poor parameter selection, or side-channel attacks.
This section presents a side-channel attack on ECDSA.

ECDSA. The domain parameters for the Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm
(ECDSA) consist of an elliptic curve E defined over a prime field Zp , chosen so that the
number n of points in E (Zp ) is prime, together with a generator point P ∈ E(Zp ). A user,
Alice, selects a secret integer a ∈R [1, n − 1] and computes the point A = aP. The point
A serves as Alice’s long-term public key, while a is her corresponding long-term private
key.
    To sign a message M, Alice first computes its hash m = H (M ). She then chooses a
per-message secret k ∈R [1, n−1], and computes the point R = kP. Let r ∈ [1, n−1] denote
the x-coordinate of R reduced modulo n. Alice also computes the integer s ∈ [1, n − 1] as

                                  s = k −1 (m + ar ) mod n.                           (130)

Alice’s signature on M is the pair of integers (r, s). Since the side-channel attack of
interest targets the signature generation process, the verification algorithm is omitted.
    For ECDSA to be secure, both the long-term private key a and each per-message se-
cret key k must be chosen uniformly at random from [1, n − 1], and a fresh value of k
must be used for every signature. In practice, however, partial information about some
§12.5 Side-channel attack on ECDSA                                                               207


per-message secrets k may leak during the signing process. Such leakage can arise from
weaknesses including poor random number generation, timing variations, electromag-
netic emanations, and so on. In some cases, the leaked information is sufficient to recover
the long-term private key a. Once a is compromised, the entire ECDSA implementation
is effectively broken.

12.6    Finding small roots of a polynomial modulo N
Univariate polynomials with integer coefficients can be efficiently factored over the in-
tegers or, equivalently, over the rational numbers. In fact, the first major application of
the LLL lattice basis reduction algorithm was a polynomial-time method for this task.
There are also randomized algorithms for factoring polynomials modulo a prime p that
run in expected polynomial time. In contrast, no efficient algorithm is known for fac-
toring polynomials modulo a composite number N ; indeed, this problem is as hard as
factoring N itself.
    In 1996, Coppersmith demonstrated that the LLL algorithm can be used to find all
sufficiently small roots of a polynomial f (x ) ∈ ZN [x], where N is a composite number
whose factorization is unknown. More precisely, for a degree-d polynomial f (x ), the
method recovers all roots x 0 satisfying |x 0 | ≤ N 1/d .
    In §12.6.1, we present Howgrave-Graham’s formulation of Coppersmith’s algorithm,
which is nonetheless commonly referred to as Coppersmith’s method. Then, in §12.6.2
and §12.6.3, we describe two applications that exploit weaknesses in some padding mech-
anisms for the RSA public-key encryption scheme.

12.6.2   RSA encryption with fixed padding
When utilizing RSA with a small public exponent e, one must be careful when encrypting
short messages. Consider the case of encryption exponent e = 3. Suppose the scheme
is used to encrypt a symmetric key K whose bitlength is much smaller than that of the
RSA modulus N . For example, N might be 2048 bits long whereas K is only 256 bits. The
resulting ciphertext is c = K 3 mod N . But since K 3 < N , reduction modulo N does not
occur, so c = K 3 . Consequently, K can be recovered simply by computing the integer
cube root of c.
     To mitigate this weakness, suppose that K is padded on the left with a string of bits,
all of which are 1, to form a message m whose bitlength is just one less than that of N .
The ciphertext is then c = m3 mod N .
     However, if the bitlength of K is less than one-third that of N , the key can still be
efficiently recovered from c. Writing m = P + K, we have c = (P + K ) 3 mod N . Thus, K
is a root of the polynomial

                          f (x ) = x 3 + 3Px 2 + 3P 2x + P 3 − c          (mod N ).

Since K < N 1/3 , it can be recovered using the Coppersmith/Howgrave-Graham method.

12.6.3   RSA encryption with random padding
To achieve security against chosen-ciphertext attacks, a plaintext message should be
randomized prior to applying the RSA encryption functions. One way to introduce this
randomness is through random padding. The following example illustrates an attack on
RSA with random right-padding.
    Let N be an RSA modulus and let e = 3 be the encryption exponent. Suppose a
message M is encrypted by first padding it on the right with a randomly selected bitstring
R of length k. Thus, the ciphertext corresponding to M is c = m3 mod N where m =
2k M + R.
    Now suppose a second encryption of the same message M is performed using in-
dependent randomness R 0 ∈R {0, 1}k , yielding m 0 = 2k M + R 0 and c 0 = (m 0 ) 3 mod N .
Assume an adversary obtains N , c and c 0. We show that the adversary can efficiently
recover M.
    Let r = R 0 − R, so that m 0 = m + r . Consider the bivariate polynomials

                  f 1 (x, y) = y 3 − c and f 2 (x, y) = (x + y) 3 − c 0 ∈ ZN [x, y].

The resultant of f 1 and f 2 with respect to y, denoted Resy ( f 1 , f 2 ), is a degree-9 polynomial
in ZN [x]:

      f (x ) = Resy ( f 1 , f 2 ) = x 9 + (3c − 3c 0 )x 6 + (3c 2 + 21cc 0 + 3(c 0 ) 2 )x 3 + (c − c 0 ) 3 .

The resultant has the following property: if, for some α ∈ ZN , the univariate polyno-
mials f 1 (α, y) and f 2 (α, y) have a common root in ZN , then f (α ) = 0. Now, f 1 (r, y) and

Coppersmith/Howgrave-Graham method can be used to efficiently determine r . Once r
is known, one can easily recover m and m 0, and hence M (Exercise 12.11).

12.7   Notes and further references
Early applications of lattice basis reduction in cryptography are surveyed by Nguyen
and Stern [170]. Lattice-based attacks on the subset sum problem were first devised
by Lagarias and Odlyzko [129] and later improved by Coster et al. [62]. Exercise 12.13
uses the Lagarias-Odlyzko attack. In 1997, Ajtai and Dwork [6] introduced a public-key
encryption scheme and proved its security based solely on the worst-case hardness of
the unique shortest vector problem (uSVP). Shortly thereafter, Nguyen and Stern [169]
presented lattice attacks showing that any secure implementation of the Ajtai-Dwork
scheme would require prohibitively large keys, rendering it impractical. Also in 1997,
Goldreich, Goldwasser and Halevi [97] proposed another lattice-based public-key en-
cryption scheme. This scheme was broken by Nguyen [162] in 1999, who showed that
decryption could be reduced to solving easy instances of the Closest Vector Problem. In
1985, Odlyzko and te Riele [174] used the LLL algorithm to disprove the Mertens con-
jecture, which posited that | n ≤x µ (n)| < x 1/2 for x ≥ 2, where µ denotes the Möbius
                               P
function. This conjecture was of interest in part because its validity would have implied
the Riemann hypothesis.
     Lenstra, Lenstra and Lovász [135] were the first to propose the use of lattice basis re-
duction for discovering integer relations. Borwein and Lisoněk [39] presented a number
of examples of relations obtained using integer relation-finding algorithms, including
LLL and PSLQ. Håstad, Just, Lagarias and Schnorr [106] introduced an integer relation-
finding algorithm, together with a detailed complexity analysis. Lehmer [134] compiled
a list of Machin-like formulae. The lattice-based method for finding simultaneous Dio-
phantine approximations described in §12.4 is also due to Lenstra, Lenstra and Lovász
[135].
     The first lattice-based attack on ECDSA that exploited the partial leakage of per-
message secrets was proposed by Howgrave-Graham and Smart [115] and further an-
alyzed by Nguyen and Shparlinski [165]. The exposition of the ECDSA side-channel
attack in §12.5 is largely based on the work of De Micheli and Heninger [67], which of-
fers a comprehensive overview of lattice-based attacks on both RSA and elliptic curve
cryptosystems. Breitner and Heninger [43] and Rowe, Breitner and Heninger [186] study
weak implementations of ECDSA signing in cryptocurrencies, including Bitcoin. Aranha
et al. [16] devised a side-channel attack targeting weaknesses in an implementation of
the Montgomery ladder used for ECDSA point multiplication. Remarkably, their lattice-
based technique succeeded even under extremely limited leakage—an average of less
than one bit of information about each per-message secret.

    The Number-Theoretic Transform (NTT) is a finite-field analogue of the Discrete
Fourier Transform (DFT). It enables the multiplication of two polynomials in the ring
Rq = Zq [x]/(x n +1) using O (n log n) Zq -operations, in contrast to the O (n2 ) Zq -operations
required by naive polynomial multiplication. The NTT is used in Kyber, Dilithium and
Falcon to accelerate polynomial multiplication in Rq , which is the dominant operation in
Kyber and Dilithium. The NTT is introduced in §13.1 and §13.2, while the specific NTT
variants used in Dilithium and Kyber are described in §13.3 and §13.4, respectively.

13.1    NTT definition
Let q be a prime number and let n ≥ 2 be an integer. Denote by Zq [x] the set of all polyno-
mials in the indeterminate x with coefficients in Zq . The quotient ring Rq = Zq [x]/(x n +
1) consists of all polynomials in Zq [x] of degree at most n − 1, with multiplication per-
formed modulo the polynomial x n +1. A polynomial a(x ) = a 0 +a 1x +· · ·+an−1x n−1 ∈ Rq
can be identified with its coefficient vector (a 0 , a 1 , . . . , an−1 ), giving a natural one-to-one
correspondence between Rq and the vector space Zqn .

Classical polynomial multiplication. Let a(x ) = a 0 + a 1x + · · · + an−1x n−1 and
b (x ) = b0 + b1x + · · · + bn−1x n−1 be elements of Rq . The classical method for computing
their product c (x ) = a(x )b (x ) mod (x n + 1) in Rq proceeds as follows:
   1. Compute the ordinary polynomial product in Zq [x]:
                            d (x ) = a(x ) · b (x ) = d 0 + d 1x + · · · + d 2n−2x 2n−2 .

   2. Reduce d (x ) modulo x n + 1 by substituting x n = −1, x n+1 = −x, . . ., and x 2n−2 =
      −x n−2 , yielding
                   (d 0 + d 1x + · · · + dn−1x n−1 ) + (−dn − dn+1x − · · · − d 2n−2x n−2 ).

   3. Add the two polynomials above to obtain c (x ) = c 0 + c 1x + · · · + c n−1x n−1 .
Steps 1 and 3 require O (n2 ) and O (n) arithmetic operations26 , respectively, for an overall
running time of O (n 2 ). In contrast, the NTT allows multiplication in Rq to be carried out
in time O (n log n).

Definition 13.1 Let n = 2k , and let q be a prime such that q − 1 is divisible by 2n. Let
ζ ∈ Zq∗ be an element of order27 2n, so that ζ n = −1. The Number-Theoretic Transform
(NTT) is the map NTT : Rq −→ Zqn defined by

                           NTT(a) = (a(ζ ), a(ζ 3 ), a(ζ 5 ), . . . , a(ζ 2n−1 )).
For notational convenience, we will often write â in place of NTT(a).
    The NTT of a(x ) evaluates the polynomial at the odd powers of ζ . These odd powers
are precisely the elements of order 2n in Zq∗ , also known as the primitive (2n)-th roots
of unity modulo q. A key property of the NTT is that it is invertible; its inverse func-
tion NTT−1 : Zqn −→ Rq can be interpreted as polynomial interpolation. Consequently,
NTT−1 (NTT(a)) = a for all a ∈ Rq .

Addition and subtraction in Rq . Let a(x ), b (x ) ∈ Rq and let c (x ) = a(x ) ± b (x ). For
any odd integer i, we have

and so ĉ = NTT(c) = â ± b̂. Thus, addition and subtraction in NTT form is component-
wise.

Fast multiplication in Rq . Let a(x ), b (x ) ∈ Rq and let c (x ) be their product in Rq , i.e.,
c (x ) = a(x )b (x ) mod (x n + 1). There exists a polynomial `(x ) ∈ Zq [x] such that
                                   c (x ) = a(x )b (x ) + `(x )(x n + 1).
For any odd integer i, we have
                        c (ζ i ) = a(ζ i )b (ζ i ) + `(ζ i )(ζ in + 1) = a(ζ i )b (ζ i ),
since ζ in = (ζ n ) i = (−1) i = −1. Therefore
            NTT(c) = ĉ = (a(ζ )b (ζ ), a(ζ 3 )b (ζ 3 ), . . . , a(ζ 2n−1 )b (ζ 2n−1 )) = â ◦ b̂,
where â ◦ b̂ denotes the componentwise multiplication of vectors in Zqn .
   In §13.2, we show that both NTT and NTT−1 can be computed in time O (n log n).
This leads to an alternative procedure for multiplying a(x ) and b (x ) in Rq :
   1. Compute â = NTT(a) and b̂ = NTT(b).
   2. Compute the componentwise product ĉ = â ◦ b̂.
   3. Recover c = NTT−1 (ĉ).
Since the componentwise multiplication requires only O (n) operations, the overall run-
ning time of this method is O (n log n), a substantial improvement over the O (n2 ) running
time of the classical method.

Recall that NTT(a) = (a(ζ ), a(ζ 3 ), . . . , a(ζ 2n−1 )). We can view the value a(ζ i ) as the
remainder obtained by dividing a(x ) by the linear polynomial x − ζ i . The algorithm for
computing the NTT uses the following result to recursively compute these remainders
by first reducing modulo higher-degree factors.

Theorem 13.2 Let a, f , д be polynomials in Zq [x]. If f divides д, then
                          a(x ) mod f (x ) = (a(x ) mod д(x )) mod f (x ).
In other words, the remainder upon dividing a(x ) by f (x ) can be obtained by first divid-
ing a(x ) by д(x ), and then dividing the resulting remainder by f (x ).

NTT running time. Let n = 2k , and let T (n) denote the time required to evaluate
NTT. We have the recursive formula

                                         T (n) = 2T (n/2) + 3n/2.

Indeed, at each level of the NTT computation tree, a total of n2 multiplications and n
additions are required to carry out the reduction steps. Moving to the next level doubles
the number of reduction steps, but each reduction operates on polynomials of half the
degree. Solving this recurrence yields T (n) = O (n log n), which is the running time of
the NTT algorithm.

13.3   Dilithium NTT
The FIPS 204 standard that specifies the Dilithium signature scheme fixes the parameters
n = 256 and q = 223 −213 +1 = 8, 380, 417, chosen so that 2n divides q−1, and the order-2n
element ζ = 1753 in Zq∗ . The associated Dilithium ring Rq = Zq [x]/(x 256 + 1) consists of
polynomials of degree at most 255 with coefficients in Z8380417 .

Dilithium NTT definition. The NTT used in Dilithium, as specified in FIPS 204, dif-
fers slightly from the transform introduced in Definition 13.1. In that earlier definition,
the components of â = NTT(a) correspond to the consecutive odd powers of ζ , namely
âi = a(ζ 2i−1 ) for 1 ≤ i ≤ n. In contrast, the Dilithium NTT permutes these powers of ζ
so that they appear in the same order as the leaves of the underlying NTT computation
tree. This avoids having to permute the values corresponding to the leaves of the NTT
tree as was done in (157).
     This ordering of leaves can be described succinctly using bit reversal. Suppose that
n = 2k . For an integer v ∈ [0, n − 1], let brv(v) = bitrevk (v) denote the k-bit integer
obtained by reversing the k-bit binary representation of v.

Definition 13.4 Let n = 2k , and let q be a prime such that q − 1 is divisible by 2n. Let
ζ ∈ Zq∗ be an element of order 2n, and define

                          ζi = ζ 2brv(i )+1 mod q for 0 ≤ i ≤ n − 1.

The Dilithium NTT is the map NTT : Rq −→ Zqn given by

                   NTT(a) = (a(ζ 0 ), a(ζ 1 ), a(ζ 2 ), . . . , a(ζn−2 ), a(ζn−1 )).

A notable feature of the NTT and its inverse is that both can be computed in-place,
requiring only minimal auxiliary storage. This is especially advantageous for hardware

13.4    Kyber NTT
The Kyber NTT parameters are n = 256 and q = 3329, so the associated polynomial
ring is Rq = Z3329 [x]/(x 256 + 1). Since q − 1 = 3328 = 28 × 13, the integer q − 1 is
divisible by n but not by 2n. As a result the standard NTT algorithm must be slightly
modified: specifically, the height of the NTT computation tree is reduced by one level.
The modified transform is called NTT2 .

NTT2 definition. Let n = 2k , and let q be a prime such that q − 1 is divisible by n but
not by 2n. Let ζ ∈ Zq∗ be an element of order n, so that ζ n/2 = −1.

Lemma 13.6 For every odd integer i ∈ [1, n − 1], the polynomial x 2 − ζ i is irreducible
over Zq .
Proof: Suppose that x 2 − ζ i were reducible over Zq . Then it would have a root c in Zq ,
implying c 2 = ζ i . Raising both sides to the n-th power gives (c 2 ) n = (ζ i ) n = (ζ n ) i = 1,
so the order of c divides 2n. On the other hand, c n = (c 2 ) n/2 = (ζ i ) n/2 = (ζ n/2 ) i =
(−1) i = −1, which shows that the order of c does not divide n. Therefore, c has order 2n,
which is impossible since 2n does not divide q − 1. This contradiction proves that x 2 − ζ i
is irreducible.                                                                                  
     For each odd integer i ∈ [1, n − 1], define the quadratic ring of polynomials
                                       Q i = Zq [x]/(x 2 − ζ i ).
Elements of Q i are polynomials of the form c 0 +c 1x with coefficients in Zq ; such a polyno-
mial can be represented by its coefficient pair (c 0 , c 1 ) ∈ Zq2 . Multiplication is performed
modulo x 2 − ζ i . The addition, subtraction and multiplication operations in Q i are the
following: if a(x ) = a 0 + a 1x, b (x ) = b0 + b1x ∈ Q i , then
                              a(x ) ± b (x ) = (a 0 ± b0 ) + (a 1 ± b1 )x,
and
                        a(x ) · b (x ) = (a 0b0 + a 1b1ζ i ) + (a 0b1 + a 1b0 )x .
Define the ring Tq as the product of the n2 quadratic rings Q 1 , Q 3 , . . . , Q n−1 :
                                   Tq = Q 1 × Q 3 × · · · × Q n−1 .
Elements of Tq can be represented as vectors in Zqn .

Kyber NTT2 . The FIPS 203 standard that specifies Kyber fixes the parameters n = 256
and q = 3329. The order-256 element ζ = 17 ∈ Z∗3329 is used. The corresponding
Kyber ring Rq = Z3329 [x]/(x 256 + 1) consists of polynomials of degree at most 255 with
coefficients in Z3329 .
     The NTT2 transform employed in Kyber, as specified in FIPS 203, differs slightly from
the transform defined in Definition 13.7. In that earlier definition, the i-th component
of â = NTT2 (a) is âi = a(x ) mod (x 2 − ζ 2i−1 ) for 1 ≤ i ≤ n2 . In contrast, the Kyber
NTT2 permutes these powers of ζ so that they appear in the same order as the leaves
of the underlying NTT2 computation tree. This avoids having to permute the values
corresponding to the leaves of the NTT tree as was done in (167).
     This ordering of leaves is concisely described using bit reversal. For an integer v ∈
[0, 127], let BitRev(v) = bitrev7 (v) denote the 7-bit integer obtained by reversing the
7-bit binary representation of v.

Definition 13.9 For 0 ≤ i ≤ 127, define ζi = ζ 2BitRev(i )+1 mod q. The Kyber NTT2 is the
map NTT2 : Rq −→ Tq defined by
         NTT2 (a) = (a mod (x 2 − ζ 0 ), a mod (x 2 − ζ 1 ), . . . , a mod (x 2 − ζ 127 )).

Kyber key generation. To generate a Kyber-KEM key pair, a user randomly selects
ρ ∈R {0, 1}256 and constructs the matrix A ∈ Rqk ×k from ρ using a pseudorandom function:
A = Expand(ρ). The user selects s ∈R Sηk1 and e ∈R Sηk1 , where Sη1 denotes the set of
polynomials in Rq all of whose coefficients lie in the interval [−η 1 , η 1 ]. The user computes
the k × 1 polynomial vector t = As + e. Their public key is (A, t ), and their private key
is s.
      NTT2 is used to accelerate the k 2 polynomial multiplications needed to compute the
matrix-vector product As. To minimize the number of NTT2 and NTT−1               2 applications,
the matrix A is generated directly in NTT2 form. Key generation proceeds as follows.

   1. Compute Â = Expand(ρ).

   2. Select s ∈R Sηk1 and e ∈R Sηk1 , and compute ŝ = NTT2 (s) and ê = NTT2 (e).

   3. Compute tˆ = Â ◦ ŝ + ê.

   4. The user’s public key is (ρ, tˆ), and their private key is ŝ.

The transforms NTT2 and NTT−1
                           2 are also used during key encapsulation and key de-
capsulation.

13.5    Notes and further references
The Number-Theoretic Transform (NTT) was introduced independently in 1971 by Nich-
olson [173], Pollard [179] and Schönhage and Strassen [191]. It can be viewed as a
finite-field analogue of the Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT), operating on sequences
of elements from a finite field rather than on sequences of complex numbers. The ear-
liest use of the NTT in lattice-based cryptography appears in the work of Hoffstein,
Pipher and Silverman [110] on NTRU, the first truly practical lattice-based cryptosys-
tem. There, the authors proposed using NTT to accelerate polynomial multiplication in
the ring Zq [x]/(x n − 1) underlying NTRU.
     The NTT variant described in §13 for polynomial multiplication in Rq = Zq [x]/(x n +
1) is tailored for so-called negacyclic convolution. The NTT used in Dilithium was in-
troduced by Ducas et al. [72]. A complete description, along with in-place algorithms
for evaluating the Dilithium NTT and its inverse, is provided in FIPS 204 [158]. The
NTT employed in Kyber first appeared in version 2.0 of the Kyber submission to NIST’s
post-quantum cryptography standardization project. A complete description, along with
in-place algorithms for evaluating the Kyber NTT and its inverse, is provided in FIPS 203
[159]. Huang et al. [116] and Zhang, Yan, Huang and Koç [204] report on software im-
plementations of Kyber and Dilithium on ARM and RISC processors.

    The definitions in this section are stated informally.

A.1     Public-key encryption
Definition A.1 A public-key encryption scheme (PKE) consists of three algorithms:

  (i) Key Generation (KeyGen) is a randomized algorithm that takes no input (or a se-
      curity parameter) and outputs a pair (EK, DK), where EK is an encryption (public)
      key and DK is a decryption (private) key.
  (ii) Encryption (Enc), which may be randomized, takes an encryption key EK and a
       plaintext message m, and outputs a ciphertext c ← Enc(EK, m).
 (iii) Decryption (Dec) takes a decryption key DK and a ciphertext c, and outputs a plain-
       text message m ← Dec(DK, c) or a distinguished failure symbol ⊥.

Correctness requirement: For every key pair (EK, DK) produced by KeyGen, every mes-
sage m, and every ciphertext c produced by Enc(EK, m), it must hold that

                                      Dec(DK, c) = m.

Definition A.2 A public-key encryption scheme is indistinguishable under a chosen-
plaintext attack (IND-CPA secure) if a computationally bounded adversary cannot dis-
tinguish between the encryptions of two equal-length messages of their choice.
    In other words, the adversary is given the encryption key EK and chooses two equal-
length messages, m 0 and m 1 . The adversary is then given a challenge ciphertext c ←
Enc(EK, mb ), where b ∈ {0, 1} is chosen uniformly at random. The adversary should be
unable to guess b correctly with a probability significantly greater than 21 .

Definition A.3 A public-key encryption scheme is indistinguishable under an adap-
tive chosen-ciphertext attack (IND-CCA2 secure) if a computationally bounded adversary
with access to a decryption oracle cannot distinguish between the encryptions of two
equal-length messages of their choice, even after receiving the challenge ciphertext.
    In other words, the adversary is given the encryption key EK and access to a decryp-
tion oracle (which decrypts ciphertexts using the corresponding decryption key DK).
The adversary chooses two equal-length messages, m 0 and m 1 , and is then given a chal-
lenge ciphertext c ← Enc(EK, mb ), where b ∈ {0, 1} is chosen uniformly at random. The
§A.2 Key encapsulation mechanisms                                                    243


adversary may query the decryption oracle both before and after receiving c, on any
ciphertext other than c itself. The adversary should be unable to guess b correctly with
a probability significantly greater than 21 .

A.2   Key encapsulation mechanisms
Definition A.4 A key encapsulation mechanism (KEM) consists of three algorithms:
  (i) Key Generation (KeyGen) is a randomized algorithm that takes no input (or a secu-
      rity parameter) and outputs a pair (EK, DK), where EK is an encapsulation (public)
      key and DK is a decapsulation (private) key.
  (ii) Encapsulation (Encaps) is a randomized algorithm that takes an encapsulation key
       EK and outputs a ciphertext c and a key K: (c, K ) ← Encaps(EK).
 (iii) Decapsulation (Decaps) takes a decapsulation key DK and a ciphertext c, and out-
       puts a key K: K ← Decaps(DK, c).
Correctness requirement: For every key pair (EK, DK) produced by KeyGen, and every
(c, K ) produced by Encaps(EK), it must hold that

                                  Decaps(DK, c) = K .

Definition A.5 A key encapsulation mechanism is indistinguishable under an adap-
tive chosen-ciphertext attack (IND-CCA2 secure) if a computationally bounded adversary
with access to a decapsulation oracle cannot distinguish the real key encapsulated in a
challenge ciphertext from a randomly chosen key, even after receiving the challenge
ciphertext.
    In other words, the adversary is given the encapsulation key EK and access to a
decapsulation oracle (which decapsulates ciphertexts using the corresponding decap-
sulation key DK). The challenger computes (c, K 0 ) ← Encaps(EK), chooses a key K 1
uniformly at random from the key space, selects b ∈ {0, 1} uniformly at random, and
gives the adversary the challenge pair (c, Kb ). The adversary may query the decapsu-
lation oracle both before and after receiving the challenge pair, on any ciphertext other
than c itself. The adversary should be unable to guess b correctly with a probability
significantly greater than 21 .

A.3   Signature schemes
Definition A.6 A signature scheme consists of three algorithms:
  (i) Key Generation (KeyGen) is a randomized algorithm that takes no input (or a se-
      curity parameter) and outputs a pair (SK, VK), where SK is a signing (private) key
      and VK is a verification (public) key.
  (ii) Signature Generation (Sign), which may be randomized, takes a signing key SK and
       a message M, and outputs a signature σ ← Sign(SK, M ).
§A.3 Signature schemes                                                                 244


 (iii) Signature Verification (Verify) takes a verification key VK, a message M, and a sig-
       nature σ , and outputs “accept” or “reject”.

Correctness requirement: For every key pair (SK, VK) produced by KeyGen, every mes-
sage M, and every signature σ produced by Sign(SK, M ), it must hold that

                              Verify(VK, M, σ ) = “accept”.

Definition A.7 A signature scheme is secure if it is existentially unforgeable under a
chosen-message attack by a computationally bounded adversary.
    In other words, given a verification key VK and access to a signing oracle (which
signs messages using the corresponding signing key SK), such an adversary should be
unable to produce a valid message-signature pair (M, σ ) for any message M not previ-
ously submitted to the oracle.
